speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the March 18, 1983, Ottawa Citizen the head of the National Research Council of Canada was reported as saying, "Man is a moral creature and what he does is necessarily moral.'' He then went on to say that moral concerns should not restrict scientists in their research.
Society must play a part in the moral concerns of scientific research, and we as legislators must play our part. But, Madam Speaker, our scientists must not abandon the moral implications of their research. To do so would be tantamount to accepting the gruesome, despicable experiments that have taken place throughout history.
We must all take responsibility for our work, whether we are scientists, legislators, or society in general.

Madam Speaker, some months ago the National Energy Board suspended its hearings into the Arctic Pilot Project on the grounds that the proponents did not have a confirmed market for their gas. Might I now add my urging to that of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) that the hearings be reconvened.
If successfully brought to fruition, the Arctic Pilot Project would create many much-needed jobs in Canada, as well as contribute sizeably to the nation's export earnings. The potentiality of prolonged delay must be jeopardizing sales negotiations with offshore customers.
There are many facets of the project which ought to be addressed by the National Energy Board and which, in reality, are largely independent of the final customer. For example, the determination of whether Arctic gas is surplus to Canadian requirements, safe production and transportation methods, northern shipping routes, environmental concerns, and the
maximization of Canadian and particularly northern benefits, do not rely on who the customer is to be.
When the national priority is the restoration of the Canadian economy-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

Madam Speaker, on Wednesday night President Reagan accused Grenada of being one of three Caribbean countries that is installing Soviet weapons and installations. To support his accusation against Grenada he showed an aerial picture of the partly built new Grenada international airport, claiming that it was taken by a United States spy plane.
As is well known, Grenada is building an international airport to support one of its major industries, tourism. Plessey Airports of Great Britain is participating in the construction with a $6.5 million contract, and France, Finland, and Venezuela have pledged assistance. The runway length, which President Reagan attacked as being too great for legitimate Grenadian use, is less than the length of the runways in the Bahamas, Curacao, Dominica Republic, Guateloupe, Martinique, Puerto Rico, Trinidad, and Barbados.
In light of the many U.S. backed invasions of Caribbean countries, such as Guatemala, Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Nicaragua, and U.S. naval manoeuvres in the Caribbean, Grenada is justifiably alarmed at the President's sabre rattling.
I, therefore, call upon the Government of Canada to state publicly that Canada will oppose any move by the United States to interfere with the sovereignty of Grenada and to assure Grenada of our support in the event of any attempt to invade that country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: QUEBEC'S REFUSAL TO PARTICIPATE IN NEED PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am taking advantage of the provisions of Standing Order 21 in

March 25, 1983
order to express to the House and to the Canadian people my feelings of dismay at the refusal of the Quebec Government to take part in the NEED program. Everyone knows that in all Quebec constituencies, there are hundreds, and in some cases even thousands, of unemployed workers who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits and are now struggling to make ends meet on welfare. For young people, that means $147 per month. The Provincial Government's constitutional nitpicking is certainly not going to help these people, who were probably hoping that the municipal authorities in their areas would at least be able to create jobs for carrying out community projects as needed. Consequently, Madam Speaker, I do hope, and I want to assure these people, that other bodies will be able to submit projects under the NEED program and that the Federal Government's $170 million will be available immediately. Yesterday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced between 300 and 400 projects. I hope that municipalities that have already submitted projects will be able to switch sponsors quickly and get organized to create jobs in their communities. These jobs are urgently needed by many people, and especially those most sharply affected by the recession.

Madam Speaker, I have been on my feet several times so far this month alone, and in most of those interventions 1 have been expressing my concerns about the Government's indifference to the plights and problems of small business. An editorial in today's The Globe and Mail underlines my concerns.
Close to half of Canada's unemployed, the editorial states, are the former employees of small and medium business. It goes on to say that "Canadians have been told of the big layoffs by big business. They have personally observed and felt the lay-offs in small and medium-sized business."
While the Government was trumpeting its leadership in economic restraint, but in fact awarding 40 per cent of its public servants raises of 10 per cent and 9 per cent, the small-business sector had imposed upon itself restraints that, in more than 30 per cent of cases, had owners taking less out of their businesses by way of personal income than they had the year before, and in another 30.6 per cent of cases taking out the same amount as they had previously. The Government's self laudatory propaganda has thus been exposed for what it is.
The depressing spectacle of Bill C-139 has, for better or for worse, passed beyond us here. It is now time for the Government to act, and act firmly, to restore confidence and credibility in the marketplace.
I urge the Minister and the Cabinet, if they wish to create recovery with the stamina it will need to sustain itself-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Madam Speaker, I wish to raise a matter that has concerned me over the last 24 hours. I read with interest and heard of the altercation that occurred yesterday outside the Chamber between those who guard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the media.
Without passing judgment on the altercation itself, since I did not see it, I would suggest that the public has the right to know what their leaders think, and what their leaders' views are on matters of public interest. There are very few ways in which this can be achieved. One method of gaining that knowledge is through the media.
It is generally acknowledged that the Prime Minister has not been dealing with the media of late and has not been making himself available for discussion or questions about matters of public interest. In my opinion, that can only lead to further altercations of the type that was reported to have occurred yesterday. I think the Prime Minister has every reason to set down some limits as to accessibility, but he must be accessible. It is an obligation of leadership that one must be accessible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TAX REVIEW-INJUSTICE AGAINST QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the House to the unfair situation of Quebecers with respect to the price of gas. I should like to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources of Canada (Mr. Chretien) to get in touch with his Quebec counterpart with a view to looking into the possibility of reviewing the matter of the progressive tax-the Parizeau-Levesque tax. Only in Quebec are motorists paying on average 59 cents for a litre of gas, as compared with 33 cents in Calgary. Quebec now levies a 16-cent tax on each litre of gasoline.
In my opinion, Madam Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources of Canada ought to make sure that Quebec does protect the interests of Quebecers because, the way it works out now, a Quebecer shells out $10 in direct taxes to the Province of Quebec each time he fills up his gas tank. That is definitely unwonted. Our energy policy is based on the
March 25, 1983

fact that all Canadians ought to be paying the same price. Keeping in mind the fact that Calgarians buy a litre of gasoline for roughly 33 cents whereas Quebecers fork out about 59 cents, we are forced to conclude that the energy policy is very good, except in Quebec where the present Government again makes all Quebecers pay for its inept administration.

Madam Speaker, all Canadians want a sound and efficient postal system. Canada Post seemed to have this as its objective. However, reality shows that its real goal is to assure for itself exclusive rights over the mail.
Canada Post's definition of a letter, with all its absurd implications, is but an attempt to solidify its absolute postal monopoly. Business and financial communities at large, including the insurance industry, with their time sensitive and urgent internal communications, will be hit the hardest in terms of reduced efficiency, added cost, and lessening of security.
Canada Post should be reminded that, despite socialistic oriented policies of the Liberal Government, we still continue to live in a free enterprise country where competition is essential to our economic growth and social well being.
It is imperative that Canada Post meets its competitors head-on instead of seeking monopolistic advantage by Government regulation. The public interest requires that Canada Post had better concentrate on improving the quality of its services and abandon policies jeopardizing our business communities already struggling to survive under the chaos introduced by the Government.
Let us hope that Cabinet will apply common sense when it considers the revised definition of a letter.

Madam Speaker, my question was to be directed to the Prime Minister but, in his absence, I will direct it to the Minister responsible for employment.
According to the latest available figures on Canadians leaving Canada, some 40,000 young people between the ages
Oral Questions
of 25 and 35 moved out of this country in the two years from 1979 to 1981.
The Conservative regime threw them out.

I think it is safe to assume that a great many of those young people left the country in order to find work. Can the Minister tell us what is being done to remove this destructive drain of young Canadian manpower and Canadian brainpower?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think we should first analyze the basic proposition put forward by the Hon. Member to determine whether people leaving the country are necessarily young people looking for work. In fact we have, on average, and have always had, about 70,000 emigrating from Canada to other places for all kinds of reasons, some for work, some to go south for retirement, and others simply to move to other locations. I would point out to the Hon. Member that, at the same time, double that number has been coming into Canada, many of them also young people coming into this country to find work and to settle here. Therefore, I really cannot answer his question when the premise is all wrong.

Madam Speaker, the Minister mentioned that
70,000	Canadians left. In fact 40,000 of those were young people between the ages of 25 and 35. If we consider the next figures, I think we will know why.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister and relates to the fact that this spring over 500,000 students will be looking for their first full-time jobs. They will be competing with the 1.5 million Canadians already looking for work, and that may explain why 40,000 left. What will the Government do about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that is a much more serious question, and I appreciate the Hon. Member bringing it forward, because there is no doubt but that the issue involving how we can help young people, those graduating from schools, to find their first jobs, is really a major national priority. I do not follow the concern raised by the Hon. Member at all. The question is: what is the best way of doing it?
We have taken a number of steps to try to provide new openings and opportunities for young people in the job market. As the Hon. Member knows, we have substantially increased training programs. We increased budgets for this fiscal year by about 20 per cent. We have substantially added to the training in the high technology and high trades areas, where there are still many job opportunities. Second, with the provincial Governments we are considering ways in which we can combine our efforts to deal with unemployment.

March 25, 1983
Oral Questions
Last January I met with provincial Ministers and put forward a policy paper for discussion. We have now held meetings with senior officials following those discussions, to find ways in which we can link up with provincial Governments in a combined effort. As I pointed out in the House yesterday and at times before, members of this caucus have been working very actively to consider a variety of ways by which we might provide incentives to the private sector, ways in which we can use federal Departments and agencies to provide first-time job opportunities.
They're so great.

Therefore, I would say that we are not immune to the issue. It is a serious issue. However, the fact is that we should recognize that the Government cannot solve the problem all by itself. It will also require major involvement by the private sector and by provincial Governments.
Sit down.

We hope that we can bring about that cooperation.
If the Leader of the Opposition is not interested in youth unemployment, then he has no business being in his seat.
Hear, hear!
Sit down!

Madam Speaker, the fact is that many of the programs which the Government has brought forward are no more than paper programs. Sixty thousand jobs were promised through the NEED Program, but to date it has created less than 15,000 jobs. Time is running out and unemployment is rising. When will the Government get after the problem and do something serious about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would again like to take the opportunity to correct the Hon. Member. The NEED Program is designed to provide jobs on an ongoing basis over an 18-month period.
For exhaustees.

We have been providing jobs at a level of
2,000	authorizations per week to ensure that we can provide work opportunities for those who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits. At the same time, through the Community Development Projects, of which the Hon. Member's own riding is a major beneficiary, we have also provided over 50,000 jobs during that period of time, so that we can provide an underlying floor foundation of direct employment opportunity.
Under the PED Program we provide incentives to the private sector to provide for wage subsidies to hire people, and
another 20,000 people are employed in those programs. Now, I do not know about the Hon. Member, Madam Speaker, but for the over 150,000 people for whom we are providing employment through direct federal forms of assistance, they are very thankful that we are providing work, rather than simply the rhetoric that they receive from the Official Opposition.

Madam Speaker, my question as well is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and is very basic.
If the Minister is so confident that his new and innovative programs are so effective, why is it that youth unemployment is rising disproportionately to the general unemployment rate? In 1979 the youth unemployment rate was 10 per cent; now it is 19.3 per cent. Of the 328,000 jobs that the Minister hopes to create this year, we already know that 20 to 25 per cent of those are five-day and two-week and three-week jobs. There are really no new ideas.
What is the Government doing to rearrange its priorities to make it possible for our young people to regain confidence in the future of the Country, and to find an employment opportunity to restore the hope and the confidence that they have a right to expect to have in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member says there are no new ideas and no new programs. I would like to point out that in the past year we introduced a work-sharing program whereby we have signed 12,000 agreements with private firms and groups of employers right across Canada that now cover close to a quarter of a million Canadian workers. We have been able to avoid over 102,000 lay-offs, and the evaluations that we have just completed indicate that that program has been supported by over 80 or 90 per cent of its users.
When the Hon. Member says that nothing new or helpful has been put in place, I would point out to him that the worksharing program, a unique program introduced by this Government, has provided major support in guaranteeing job security.
At the same time, I do not quarrel with the concern that Members of this House have expressed about young people coming into the job market. It is unquestionably one of the most serious issues we face, and the reason is because we are still in the midst of a recession, a world-wide recession, where companies, rather than hiring a first-time worker, will be hiring people that they had laid off. Those people will be given the first opportunities, and therefore the companies will not be giving the first-time workers a chance to get on the job.
We must find ways of dealing with the problem; there is no question about that. But I will argue and quarrel with the Hon.
March 25, 1983

Member's statement that nothing has been done. We have been sitting down with provincial Governments and with private business to find how we can recruit and enlist their cooperation. We would do the same with Members opposite, as we would like to be able to get ideas from them. Rather than their being simply critical, if they have good ideas we are prepared to listen to them, because we have a number of ideas coming from our own caucus.
Hear, hear!
Madam Speaker, our frustration stems precisely from the fact that the Government has refused to accept any new and innovative ideas from us, and examples from other countries.
Hear, hear!
Madam Speaker, of all the countries with which we compare our statistics-
Name one.

-our record is definitely the worst in terms of youth unemployment. There will be 600,000 young people flooding out of the gates of our schools and universities during the next few weeks. Very few of them will find a meaningful first work experience.
Why is the Government so stubborn? Why has it not accepted some of the innovative suggestions that we have made to it to stimulate and entice the small business sector to make work for young people and, in so doing, find a means to survive the economic holocaust that the Government has created?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the reasons is because we find the suggestions coming from the Hon. Members opposite to be so confusing. One day they say that the Government's deficit is too high, that it is spending too much money, that it should slash its programs and cut its expenditures. The next day the Hon. Member is saying that we should bring in new programs and make more expenditures.
As soon as the Official Opposition is able to decide what it wants to do, then we would be more prepared to listen. But as long as its members are speaking with 12, 13 or 14 voices, we cannot figure out what they mean.
At the same time I would point out to them that, in terms of working with the private sector, the NEED Program has received applications, and something like 20 or 30 per cent of the work programs are now working with private sector firms. I could give one example. The Hon. Member for St. John's East is not here, but we just signed an agreement with a company in his constituency. They are putting up $4 million and we are putting up half a million dollars. We are putting
Oral Questions
120 people back to work, working with the private sector. That is the kind of leadership we are giving, not simply the noise from the left-hand corner of the Chamber over there.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will not ask the Minister to repeat his answer.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext: He will anyway.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext:
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. There are two bits of alarming news in the press today. First, the chief economist of the Conference Board indicated that real unemployment is about 18 to 20 per cent, which means that there are approximately 700,000 more Canadians unemployed than the Government figures indicate. The other information comes from Statistics Canada. More particularly, an official speaking on that data said that the so-called recovery that is to come in 1983 will be the lowest since World War II. Both of these mean that unemployment in 1983, unless the Government does something quickly to stimulate the economy, will be as bad as it has been for the past year.
Will the Minister tell us the date of the budget, and will he promise that there will be major measures in his budget to stimulate the production of jobs?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as far as the date of the budget is concerned, I certainly hope to be able to inform the House before we adjourn for Easter of the date for the budget speech. As far as the Hon. Member's second question is concerned, I am working on a budget that I hope will stimulate the economy, help with the creation of jobs in this country, and speed up the recovery. With regard to the premise of the Hon. Member's question, I remind him that there are many economists with many views.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING DATE OF BUDGET PRESENTATION
speechtext: There are many economists with many views, and almost without exception all the reports that come from private sector sources, as well as Government information for the past two weeks, say one thing, and one thing only, that more than two million Canadians will remain without a job in 1983 unless the Government starts to act. That is what they agree on.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister in terms of action the Government could take now to stimulate the economy. It

March 25, 1983
Oral Questions
concerns energy pricing. The Minister's colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Ressources, has indicated we may have to wait until July to see enforcement of the oil-pricing agreement, which means that prices for the Canadian consumer which should now be about ten cents a gallon lower, will not be brought down until then at the earliest. If we enforce that agreement now, ten cents a gallon could translate into about
33,000	additional jobs for Canadians. Will the Minister tell us why he is waiting until July? Why is the Government postponing this action? Why does it not take steps to bring down those prices now?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first, the desire for action is indeed very widespread. As the Hon. Member knows, the problem, whether it is between economists, business people or forecasters, is that there is a very large amount of disagreement as to what steps should be taken. Some say enlarge the deficit, some say don't. Some say have more Government spending, some say no, let the economy-

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
speechtext: What do you say?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
speechtext:
The Hon. Member will have to wait for my budget to find out what I have to say.
I do not think it is fair for the Hon. Member to assume that the points of view expressed are as uniform as he attempts to indicate. As far as the agreement with Alberta is concerned, surely the Hon. Member knows that the agreement specifically provides that there is an adjustment of prices every six months, whether the prices come down or go up. When prices were going up, Alberta was asked, and agreed, to wait six months. Twice a year there were adjustments in the price of oil. That still applies, whether the prices go up or come down. Surely the Hon. Member is not advocating that we should unilaterally break an agreement, not respect our word and commitment in that regard, and not abide by the agreement. We intend to abide by the agreement. My hon. friend will have to wait until July for the particular decisions to be taken.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT REDUCE OIL PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all, as to the agreement, the Minister, as I have understood him, is incorrect. The agreement does provide procedures which would enable the Government to move upward in terms of prices, if the world price changed in an upward direction, every six months. It also permits action to be taken during that six-month period if Governments want to act. The Minister knows that there would be no violation of the agreement at all if the two Governments involved took action now to bring down those prices to what Canadian consumers ought to be experiencing at this point.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEW JOB CREATION MEASURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like now to come to my last question. Each week there are approximately 20,000 men and women coming off unemployment insurance. Many of these thousands of people are being driven to welfare. Quite independently of those who are being forced to go on welfare, there are thousands of other Canadians who, for different reasons, are going on the welfare rolls. Does the Minister and the Government not recognize some urgency to take action in terms of job creation? Can he not announce some additional specific measure before the Easter break, instead of us having to wait for the budget, in order to get some more jobs in our economy?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEW JOB CREATION MEASURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am glad that the Hon. Member admits we should not take unilateral action with regard to the agreement. He says that the Governments are obviously free to agree to make a change to the agreement-

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEW JOB CREATION MEASURES
speechtext: Not a change to the agreement.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEW JOB CREATION MEASURES
speechtext:
-or to agree to proceed with price changes under the agreement. But it requires the agreement of both Governments. I can tell the Hon. Member that the Government of Alberta and the other producing Provinces have not agreed to such changes at the present time. My colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, met with his colleague, the Minister from Alberta, last week. Further discussions are taking place. If and when any decisions are arrived at, I am sure the Minister of Energy will be very happy to communicate them to the House.
As far as the announcement of additional programs, or additional expenditures, is concerned, I remind my hon. friend that we have already some $2 billion worth of direct job creation programs in one form or another, or training programs, in operation at the present time. There are funds which have been approved and the processing is taking place of the various applications, as the Minister of Employment and Immigration has announced. We are trying to speed up that process as much as we can in order to accommodate the largest possible number of unemployed. We are quite conscious and quite concerned about the situation raised by my hon. friend. We are trying to cope with it as fast as we can. If there are other measures to be announced, however, they will be part of the budget.

subsubtopic: RAILWAY STATION AT MINAKI, ONT -POSSIBLE TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. For about the last six to eight months there have been negotiations
March 25, 1983

going on between the Minaki Corporation, CN, Via Rail, and the Department of Transport over the transfer of a former railway building at Minaki to the Minaki Corporation. I am sure the Minister will agree that eight months is a long time for Crown corporations to get their act together. With the opening of Minaki Lodge taking place within the next month, could the Minister say whether he will intervene to make sure that this charade is ended?

subsubtopic: RAILWAY STATION AT MINAKI, ONT -POSSIBLE TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
speechtext: Madam Speaker, Via has been preparing a program for the restoration of stations for a number of months, if not years. It is a rather expensive proposition. This program has not been approved by the Treasury Board yet, but realizing the urgency of the matter put forward by my hon. friend, and realizing that the Government of Ontario has restored the Minaki Lodge and would like to have control of the station, I have made a very dramatic decision, a strong decision.

subsubtopic: RAILWAY STATION AT MINAKI, ONT -POSSIBLE TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RAILWAY STATION AT MINAKI, ONT -POSSIBLE TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
speechtext: As usual. Discussions are going on now between CN and Via Rail for the transfer of the station. In the coming weeks, then, there will be an agreement, I dare say, between Via and the Government of Ontario in order to accommodate the desire of the government of Ontario to lease the station.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister has stated that the Government owes 11 million Canadians about $6.5 billion in tax refunds, and now that the Income Tax Act has passed the House the tax refunds will go out next month. Does the Minister have the cash on hand to pay the tax refunds which he owes Canadians, or does he have to borrow it?

Madam Speaker, the borrowing authority Bill which is before the House has a good chance of being passed by the end of this particular part of the Session, that is, before Easter. Thanks to the generosity of Parliament, I am sure there will be plenty of money. As to whether that money comes from money borrowed or from money coming in from tax receipts, we do not stamp dollars saying that it is a borrowed dollar, or that it is a tax dollar. The money will come out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. My hon. friend need not worry; she will get her tax refund if she has applied for it. I will not be able to tell her, however, if it is coming from borrowings or from actual cash reserves of the Government.

What reserves?
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. Canadians can count on the fact that one dollar out of every three dollars the Government spends is a borrowed dollar. The Government is so broke that it is borrowing money under emergency powers which, as far as we can determine, have never been used before. By next Thursday the Government will have borrowed, through the back door, about $2.3 billion without the authority of Parliament. What steps is the Government taking, aside from seeking to borrow another $19 billion, to get itself out of this emergency situation?

Madam Speaker, the hon. lady is creating a phony emergency. The money which has been borrowed has been borrowed under the authority of Parliament. It has been borrowed under the Borrowing Authority Act, Section 39. It has been passed by this Parliament. The action which has been taken has been taken completely under the authority provided by this Parliament.
I am also pleased to inform the Hon. Member that the Receiver General has advised me that he currently has $5 billion in cash to pay a good part of those refunds, so I do not believe she has to worry. We will not go bankrupt over the weekend. We will still be here next Monday. And we will have plenty of time to pass the borrowing authority legislation. The Hon. Member need not fear. I wish her a very good weekend.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The Minister will know that the CTC scheduled hearings to inquire into the benefit of, or the detriment of the participation of CNR and Cast as fellow businessmen. In the last six months CNR obtained two delays of those hearings to determine whether or not this was in fact a good thing for Canada. Will the Minister confirm that, while these delays were taking place, the CNR has in fact purchased Cast, and this has been announced by Lloyds Registry of Shipping in London, England?

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend, and others, always speak as if the CTC has never looked at the Cast acquisition, or the CN participation in Cast. The CTC has done that twice, and has agreed with it, generally speaking-at least once, I must correct myself. On the subject of the discussions between CN and Cast and Sofati, at this time I am not in a position to answer. I do not think there has been any conclusive decision yet. I would like to repeat, though, very emphatically, that whatever decision is arrived at is subject to the approval of Cabinet and is subject to the approval of the CTC.

March 25, 1983
Oral Questions

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF PRIVATE ENTERPRISE
QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF PRIVATE ENTERPRISE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the trend and policy of the Government have been to encourage socialist participation in the transportation industry. I would now like to direct another question to the Minister of Transport.
When is the Minister going to establish a climate in which private enterprise might participate in the deep-sea shipping interests of Canada, and when is he going to investigate the viability which has already been proven, but should be announced, of the Ports of Saint John and Elalifax for 12 months of the year as open Ports, windows to the international world of trade for Canada on a very viable basis, and recognize as well the socialist tendencies of the CNR and their interests?

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING ROLE OF PRIVATE ENTERPRISE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is not much that has to do with philosophy here. The two reasons why CN is interested in being in Cast or in an organization of that type are simply because of the importance of multi-modalism in transportation today. Everyone will tell you that it is very important for a carrier to be associated with others, or to own others in other modes of transportation, if you want to have the door-to-door service for which Cast was known. That is one point, and I repeat, it does not have anything to do with theology or philosophy. It is reality.
The second reason is that in the Port of Montreal today CP has acquired a very strong position, both on rail and on water. So if my hon. friend does not want CN to be left behind, CN has to compete, and it has to compete with CP on similar terms, hence the interest of CN in staying in Cast or in acquiring other facilities.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment. Unemployment in British Columbia has reached 196,000, and communities like Kamloops should be declared national disaster areas for purposes of emergency job creation. The Minister is aware that the B.C. Government is exploiting this human tragedy with misleading, exaggerated, and inaccurate public advertising, claiming the credit for thousands of jobs which do not exist, and also for federal programs for which it has not had the responsibility.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport who, I am sure is aware of the serious difficulties Canadian grain producers are facing as a result of low world prices and the price cutting policies of the United States and the European Economic Community. This has led to the threat of a massive reduction in the initial price of grain paid to prairie producers. Is the Minister's Government actively considering taking any action in this particular area and, if so, what action is being contemplated?

Madam Speaker, I see three parts to the answer. The first one is that, indeed, we take exception to some of the marketing tactics that the Americans have used, particularly in Iraq, for example, which is a cash market, and where they have made sales recently using blended credit. We do not think that is cricket, so we have made a protest on that subject.
The second point is that, contrary to the impression given by my hon. friend, recently there has been in the grain markets of the world a certain strengthening of Canadian Red Spring No. 1, for example, which sold at $204 a ton about ten days ago, is selling at $217 today, and at $222 the day before. So there has been an interesting upward trend. I do not want to make too much of it. On the surface one of the reasons is the limitation of cultivated acreage in the United States. Another reason has been the apparent relatively poor crop in the Soviet Union. "Le malheur des uns fait le bonheur des autres".
Thirdly, on the subject of initial prices, indeed we studied the subject yesterday in committee of Cabinet, so it is on its way to Cabinet now and an announcement should be made in the coming days.

Madam Speaker, in light of this so-called strengthening in the market can we expect that the initial price will remain at the level of the 1982-1983 initial price, or higher? Secondly, what action, in addition to a mere protest, is the Government taking to encourage co-operation among the major exporting nations of the world so that there can be some stability in the pricing arrangements for the grain industry as a whole?

Madam Speaker, on the second question, 1 have nothing much to add to what the Hon. Member knows. Canada constantly makes an effort to bring producer and consumer countries together internationally, but without great success in recent years. One has to add the years when my hon. friend was Minister of Transport in terms of the lack of success in recent times.
On the subject of the level of initial payments, my hon. friend is very learned in these matters. I am aware of that, and

He said: Madam Speaker, we are taking up the report stage of Bill C-130 and discussing the amendment which stands in my name on the Order Paper and presented on behalf of this Party. At the outset, may I say that the wording of the amendment was arrived at following discussions. I believe it is the intention of the Government to accept my amendment. In a few moments we will hear from the spokesperson for the New Democratic Party, and I have some reasons to believe that that Party also finds the amendment acceptable. In this case, I believe it would be in the interests of speedy passage of the legislation if my intervention were brief.
Bill C-130 was debated on second reading in November and extensive discussions were held in committee in December. We are now going to discuss the amendment and what it seeks to do to the Bill.
Let me remind the House that the principle of the Bill is to provide for transitional payments of some $442,000 to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue fund, and $117,040,000 to be issued in the form of non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes to the eight regional lending institutions listed in the Schedule of the Act.
One of the reasons for the importance of debating this legislation is the fact that it is a very rare occasion when the House is seized of any sort of debate on these matters, let alone dealing with legislation having to do with Canada's role in international development. As we know, CIDA has been operating through the years without an Act of Parliament. The only time we deal in any substantial way with CIDA does as the main proponent of Canada's role in international development, is at the time of the Estimates. I am afraid that all Members of the House are too well aware of the inadequacy of the rules concerning the examination of Estimates that preclude the full treatment that important spending programs require.
Spokesmen for this Party have previously expressed the basic support that we bring to the Bill. We believe that the sums mentioned in the Bill, and indeed the Bill's thrust, are in harmony with Canada's role in international development. It reflects the concerns of many Canadians that Canada play a proper role in international development, both bilaterally and multilaterally, not to mention the role of supporting nongovernmental organizations that, in my view, perform perhaps the most valuable work toward human development programs in the world on a dollar for dollar basis.
Nevertheless, this Bill deals with part of Canada's commitment to multilateral agencies and specifically to international financial institutions. Since we have made commitments to those institutions, there is no doubt that the correct procedure to follow would be to pass this Bill after recognizing the work we have done in the House today and the consideration we have given to its principles and limitations during the second reading and committee stages.
We are now seeing an important qualification. The Bill as presented to us would have allowed the Government to change the names of financial institutions by Order in Council, particularly the eight that are named in the Bill. For the purpose of the record, I should briefly refer to those institutions. They are: the African Development Fund, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Fund, The Asian Development Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, the Fund for Special Operations of the Inter-American Development Bank, the Caribbean Development Bank and Special Development Fund, the International Fund for Agricultural Development, and now the new Common Fund for Commodities that has evolved from the discussions of UNCTAD over the past few years.
The amendment before us addresses itself precisely to the problem of how the names of those institutions would be changed. As I have said, whereas the present Bill would allow the Government to do this by Order in Council without its being subject to the scrutiny of Parliament, the amendment would provide that if the Government decided to alter that list, to add or substract, but particularly to add, it would bring such an order before Parliament and put it in the form of a motion to which Members of Parliament could address themselves. To do this, 30 Members of Parliament would be required to sign a statement that would call for a special three-hour debate, to be followed by a vote. That procedure would allow Members of Parliament to fulfill at least a modicum of responsibility in scrutinizing where Canada's money is going.
As I have indicated, the wording of the amendment was arrived at after consultations and discussions. I believe it to be a good amendment. Moreover, there are several precedents for such an amendment which provides that 30 Members of Parliament sign a statement calling for debate on a motion that the Government is required, by legislation, to bring forward when it seeks to change certain Bills that have been passed by the House in any substantive way.
The precedent for my amendment is found in Bills C-102 and C-123. The wording in both those Bills is almost identical to that found in the amendment before us. Those amendments have previously found favour with the House and have established a precedent which I believe the House would be wise to follow today at the report stage of the present Bill. Having said that, I want to make two brief comments.

I think the House would be interested to know that there were several questions raised in committee about the procurement by Canadian business from those international institutions to which we are subscribing funds. Subsequent to the committee hearings in December, I received some very interesting information from Mr. Bill McWhinney, the Acting President of CIDA, which I think is useful and ought to be put on the record now. 1 am informed that the returns to Canada from the money that we put into these international financial institutions amounts to a 66 per cent return. The latest figures that are available show that Canada has received some $930.4 million in procurement which is related to Canadian contributions of $1.4 billion.
I would also bring some additional information to the attention of Hon. Members which relates to the downstream commercial benefits to many firms that have tendered and received contracts from international financial institutions. I specifically refer to the study done by the Asian Development Bank that confirms that although the level of Canadian bidding remains low on a relative basis, the success rate of Canadian bids tendered is generally high. More important, it is noted that there is an ongoing effort to generate interest and increased awareness by Canadian companies in the IFI financed projects through a series of conferences, seminars and promotional tours across Canada by IFI procurement officials.
The World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank have all conducted tours within the last 18 months. Financial assistance to Canadian firms seeking export contracts, including those financed by the IFI, is also available.
Therefore, we see that some progress is being made on procurement by Canadian firms, although I do not believe it is yet at a substantial level. I urge the Government to do more to help Canadian business achieve those contracts and obtain that legitimate business that follows from the greater flow of Canadian assistance and contributions in the form of loans and grants into the multilateral institutions. If we are to play a greater role, as we have been asked to do in the Brandt Report and the many professional studies that have been conducted, we will have to ensure that Canadians, and particularly Canadian business, receive their fair entitlement to the benefits that will increase development throughout the world. This will be done when we recognize the need for increased international financing today to solve the debt crisis, when we recognise the need for the doubling of the bases of the IMF and the World Bank and the increase of facilities to make more of the world's liquidity available in those areas of the world that are pressed for development now and are caught in the international debt crisis.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take part in the debate on Bill C-130 for several reasons. The most important of these is my involvement in the area of international development and the study my colleagues and
Financial Institutions
myself have made on all aspects of our relations with the countries of Fatin America and the West Indies.
Mr. Speaker, another reason why I wanted to take part in this debate concerns the selection or evaluation of the borrowing projects which have been submitted by various countries. What I mean, Mr. Speaker, is that I am concerned that the ministers of the various countries which contribute to the international financial institutions are not really in charge. The politicians are not sufficiently involved in the selection and evaluation of the borrowing projects. Very often, Canada finds itself in a situation where one of the institutions to which we contribute funds grants a loan to a country which, at least in our opinion, is not sufficiently respectful of human rights. Because of this, Canadian contributions to these international institutions are often used to help countries which we should not necessarily be helping and I find it unfortunate that the politician responsible, whether the Minister of Finance of Canada (Mr. Lalonde) or the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), would be directly involved in the selection and assessment of loan proposals which are made to us through those financial institutions.

Also, this legislation provides for continuing financial assistance by Canada to a number of international financial institutions which play a vital role in Third World development. My predecessor and friend, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), gave the list of the institutions. I will not repeat them. I am confident that the vast majority of Hon. Members of this House understand and appreciate the importance of international development and the seriousness of the crisis facing the Third World countries and people as a result of the current economic recession. To take only one example, Mexico is undergoing harsh and severe adjustments as the result of its balance of payments problems.
I am equally confident that most Hon. Members now understand that it is in Canada's self interest, as well as being our moral obligation, to remain firmly committed to development and improved North-South relations. It is particularly worthy of note that leading members of the Canadian business community have been drawing attention to the importance of these matters. For example, Mr. William Mulholland, Chairman of the Bank of Montreal, recently observed that "loans to the developing countries represent investments in the future health of the entire world's trading system".
The first thing to be noted about these financial institutions is that they are not in the business of giving money away. They are carefully managed institutions, mostly dealing in loans to the Third World countries. The record of repayment over the years has been excellent, which is why the banks are able to raise capital themselves on the most favourable commercial terms.
At the same time, the regional development banks, such as the World Bank, have special funds or "windows" which provide loans at lower than commercial rates to the poorest countries in the world. In this way and in their project selection they attempt to deal with the problem of mass poverty. As

March 25, 1983
Financial Institutions
the parliamentary Task Force on North-South Relations concluded, investment in the overcoming of poverty and misery is one of the best long-term investments we can make.
One measure of the competence and effectiveness of the international financial institutions was provided by a 1981 study by the U.S. Treasury Department of the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the African Development Fund. I think all Hon. Members will agree that the U.S. Treasury Department is not a soft-hearted or soft-headed organization, and yet this study found that the institutions were generally well run and effective in promoting development. It concluded that continued U.S. participation was justified by a fundamental national interest in a more stable and secure world.
During the course of my own work over the past three years with the parliamentary Task Force on North-South Relations and the Subcommittee on Canada's Relations with Fatin America and the Caribbean, I have had occasion to study and meet with officials of many of the institutions listed in Bill C-130.
While I have no doubt that there are areas of their work which can and should be improved, I am also convinced that they serve important Canadian interests. I would summarize these as follows: First, they serve to expand private financing and investment through co-financing and participation in projects for which they do the basic staff and analysis work. Second, they encourage efficient use of local resources. Third, they are in the forefront of research on development problems and policies, particularly in the area of basic human needs. Fourth, they expand and enhance the value of Canadian aid through CIDA's participation in large-scale projects planned by the international financial institutions. Fifth, the regional banks provide excellent opportunities for Canada to develop commercial and other contacts with Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa and Asia. These regional markets are among the most promising for long term expansion of Canadian trade. Sixth, they provide an immediate market for Canadian goods and services. While it has been noted that the Canadian procurement record is poorer than that of some other countries, studies show that Canadian suppliers and consultants do very well when they bid on contracts. In short, we need to get out and hustle for this business.
I would conclude as I began, by arguing that immediate selfinterest as well as our fundamental commitment to development should and will lead this House to give strong support to Bill C-130.

Mr. Speaker, we have agreed that there will be just one Hon. Member speaking per Party, covering both report stage and third reading stages of the Bill. On behalf of the New Democratic Party I say that although we are supporting the Bill as we did on second reading, and certainly supporting the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), we do, and I do particularly, have some quite serious reservations about it.
At the time of second reading I requested the Government to bring to the standing committee a detailed report from the Canadian perspective on the operation of each of the eight institutions mentioned in the appendix to the Bill, and particularly concerning the operations of the Inter-American Development Bank. However, we received no detailed reports on the operations of the institutions concerning which we are voting today to replenish the Canadian contribution. There was nothing in writing prepared and there was nothing verbal offered.
Referring to my speech on November 9, 1982, during second reading stage, I expressed some of our Party's very serious reservations which, in effect, concerned the political criteria being used in deciding, with particular reference to the InterAmerican Development Bank, what countries would be granted loans. I suggested that the Minister might bring to the Committee a more detailed review of the criteria used in the granting of loans. Again, there was no satisfactory response to this concern, a concern which is shared by other Members of the House as well.
The Hon. Member who just spoke mentioned but did not elaborate upon the situation of large loans going to countries engaged in massive violations of human rights. That was one of the criteria that I asked about. A second one that I asked about was when loans are in effect being used by Government forces, so-called security forces, to further engage in a civil war or in a war of aggression against a neighbour.
I wanted to have some analysis from the Government as to whether or not we should be engaging in the support by a multilateral institution like the Inter-American Development Bank when that is the kind of way in which the money is being used. I had already written to the Minister about this in connection with the loan to Guatemala.
The third point on which I had requested further enlightenment was whether we should be looking to see whether the loans were really directed to satisfying basic human needs and whether they should be conditioned, to at least some extent, on the degree to which they satisfied these basic human needs and addressed the problem of the very serious maldistribution of income in many of the countries that are recipients of loans.
I was really extremely disappointed on the fact that the Government has failed to address these issues seriously. The Minister of course paid no attention to them whatsoever, but I was sorry that the Department or CIDA did not address these requests a bit more fully. In fact, they hardly addressed them at all.
That being the case, although we will support report stage and third reading of this Bill, I think it only fair to say that we do it now with really very great reservations for the reasons I have given. By the way, Mr. Speaker, my reservations have increased because of new evidence that the Inter-American Development Bank is becoming, I am sorry to say, an agent of White House policy in Latin America and particularly in
March 25, 1983

Central America, and the recent loans to El Salvador, to which we have contributed, give ample evidence of this.
I am sure some Hon. Members will have already read the report, which was mentioned by The Globe and Mail on March 24, 1983, of James Morrell of the Center for International Policy in Washington, a centre which monitors U.S. policy in the Third World. It is quite clear from his report that indeed political considerations are becoming even more critical in the final decision on who gets what loans from the InterAmerican Development Bank. The political considerations, I am sorry to say, seem to have nothing to do with human rights violations; they have nothing to do with redistribution of income and they have nothing to do with whether or not the money is being spent on arms. All they have to do with, it seems, is whether or not the recipient country is one that is favoured by the U.S. State Department in its, to put it mildly, reactionary policies vis-a-vis Central America.
We must look more seriously than we have done at the Canadian contribution to loans being given to various countries by such an international financial institution as the InterAmerican Development Bank, and ask some very serious questions. It is not good enough for the Minister to say, as he did to me, that they do not consider political considerations in the granting of loans, when it has become very clear that when the Americans say no to Inter-American Development Bank loans to Nicaragua but yes to loans to El Salvador, a political consideration is in fact being made.
I think that the amendment which the Hon. Member introduced, and which we support, that the Government cannot add to or subtract from the list or the schedule, is a useful amendment and will, if 30 Members so request, give us an opportunity for debate. However, I now feel that since there was such an inadequate response to my concerns and to the concerns of other Members on the criteria used in the giving of loans, we have to find some other method, before we are next asked for a Canadian replenishment, of ensuring that we get complete reports on the activities of every agency, and that we follow them with a careful and thorough examination and discussion of the criteria that are used in the granting of loans and, finally, that we ascertain that in fact political considerations do not enter into what are supposed to be neutral decisions.
We have agreed on one speaker, so I guess I will not get my answer now, but I would hope that the Government will take my suggestions very seriously into consideration.

speechtext:
The objective of the Bill before us, which it is our intention on this side to support and deal with expeditiously so that it can be dealt with in the appropriate Committee, is to extend the provision of the Small Businesses Loans Act for an additional period of two years. The provisions of the Act were to have expired on March 31, 1983 and the intention of this Bill is to extend that period of time to March 31, 1985 and to allow the volume of loans to be guaranteed within that period to be made up to a maximum of $1.5 billion.
What I just said should have been said by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey), whom I see in his seat, in order to show the real intention of the Bill. I want to address one point fairly briefly, that is, the difference in philosophy on this side of the Chamber and the other side as to how we might have handled things differently. On the specifics, other Members on this side will go into the details.
The Minister of State responsible for Small Businesses knows what is happening. He was formerly the Minister of National Revenue. His revenue procedures worsened the plight of small businesses, and today he is trying to put that right. Today he is paying his penance, so to speak. The idea of the Government, in its grab for more and more revenue, is to hit hard the business sector of Canada. It is supported in this by our friends to the extreme left, only one of whom is here today because they do not like the idea of business making profits.
We saw this in Bill C-139 which was enforced by closure yesterday. This will hurt small business. We see the 12.5 per cent small business dividend distribution tax and the way that will affect small-businessmen. The provisions of Bill C-139 and

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
the budgets will no longer permit small businesses to participate in certain deferred profit-sharing plans. That will affect the revenues and profits of small businesses. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has stated that he intends to tax benefits that are commonly accepted in Northern parts of Canada, such as Labrador City represented by the Minister who will be speaking later today.
I want to speak specifically on the taxation of northern benefits. They affect large corporations such as the Iron Ore Company of Canada. This is one more straw on the camel's back in those types of operations. It will affect federal, provincial and territorial Governments which will have to find additional moneys with which to recompense their employees who will be subject to this additional taxation. Probably more than anything, it will affect the small northern businessman, the guy whose profit is limited, whose every dollar counts.
When new taxes are placed on the employees or the proprietor of a small business, it makes life doubly difficult. I suspect that a disproportionate number of northern small businesses will go into receivership compared to the number elsewhere in Canada if this provision in the budget announced last year by the Minister of Finance goes into effect.
Other Members on this side will speak of the necessity for skilled help, certain financing arrangements which could be worked out, the regulations and paper burden placed on small businesses, the way that Government purchasing and procurement policies could be used to assist small business. On one hand the Government is putting an additional burden on small businesses, whether it be a financial burden by way of additional taxation or more regulations and paper work, grabbing all it can and taking it away, and with the other hand with this type of legislation trying to give a little assistance back to them.
My preference is allowing market forces to operate on their own. It would not be necessary for the Government to bring forward complicated pieces of legislation designed to assist businesses, small businesses in particular, if it were not taking everything away from them at the same time. The market would operate much more smoothly. We cannot protect every small-businessman. Some will go out of business. Some are in the wrong business, some do not work as hard as others and some experience bad luck. The small business sector as a whole would be healthier and more productive if we as Parliamentarians, people who impose legislation, were to rearrange our thinking. We should allow the market to operate freely and smoothly instead of impeding it, sometimes with good intentions.
In the remaining minutes I want to bring to the attention of this House some matters that affect small business and banking, particularly in the area I represent, the Northwest Territories. A lot of what I will say has been brought to my attention by my constituents, but may be equally applicable in other northern areas of Canada, and in fact throughout the country. There is suspicion in my area that those who control the banking operations from head offices or regional offices in the South do not really appreciate the special needs of business in northern Canada. Take the present economic climate over
much of southern Canada and in parts of the North, and you find that business is at a standstill. One can understand the reason why a banker would not want to force more loans on people, if they ever do that, and why people are a little more cautious than normal. However, in areas such as the Mackenzie Delta, the Mackenzie River and Norman Wells, where there is a lot of oil exploration and development gearing up for production, the businesses there need more money. They can handle further indebtedness in a prudent manner. This would allow them to expand and take advantage of the increasing economic opportunities which exist in that part of the country. It is suspected that this is not known in southern head offices of the banks. Local loan offices are not permitted to authorize on their own account sufficient funds required to operate a business where it is necessary to keep large inventories because of the transportation difficulties and high transportation costs. For example, the freight on a truckload of flour from the mills of Edmonton or Calgary to the Mackenzie Delta is about $10,000, which is the maximum amount a local loan officer can authorize. Therefore, a baker cannot buy a truckload of flour on credit without the banker contacting the head office in Edmonton or Calgary. He cannot pay the freight on that truckload of flour, let alone purchase the contents.
Mortgage money is especially hard to come by in northern parts of Canada. That has been made known to me on several occasions. In some areas there are no banking services whatsoever. For example, in the hamlet of Fort Rae-Edzo, with a population of 1,500 to 2,000 people, there is no bank. The nearest bank is 60 or 70 miles away. I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for one of the chartered banks to move into a town like that. There is more and more money all the time coming into these towns, and there is a tremendous opportunity to grow with them. It might take a few years before the branch of the bank makes a profit, but there does exist an opportunity for the banking community, an opportunity which should be seized, and which will also provide proper banking service in locations where that is not presently available.
There are cases, and one of these happened very recently in the Town of Inuvik, where a previous bank manager had been suspected by his head office of being a little too lenient and giving out too much money to business, small business in particular, by way of loans. He was subsequently replaced and the new manager was told to tighten up right away. It may be true that the previous manager was handing out too much money, but I believe investigations are showing that this is exaggerated. However, when someone new comes in to a small town bank and immediately changes the policy, refuses to allow extensions to lines of credit, calls in loans, or starts bouncing cheques, the whole business community suffers the repercussions.
You can imagine what would happen if this were to occur nationally, because any banking system which relies on fractional reserves is inherently insolvent. Once that sort of
March 25, 1983

thing starts happening, the very thing which the banking industry most fears is precipitated. Unless credit policies are changed gradually over a period of time, the local business community is subjected to much greater difficulty than it should experience, and there are real problems and occasionally bankruptcies.
Another complaint has been made known to me by people who deal with oil companies which are the recipients of PIP grants. The Government has decided that it is in the national interest to pay large numbers of taxpayers' dollars to oil companies in order to allow them to operate in remote areas. This is deemed to be in the national interest. Effectively, therefore, companies such as Dome Petroleum can be operating with what amounts to 25-cent dollars, and in the days of the Gallagher amendment and super depletion it was a lot less than that. In turn, the local small business community feels that those recipients of Government largesse should help to spread some of that wealth, instead of taking such a hard line and insisting that everyone be absolutely competitive. Because they have been given assistance themselves to operate in remote areas, it is believed they should in turn assist those permanent resident businesses in the same way. This is not always seen to happen.
The Federal Business Development Bank has received a number of suggestions as to the way they could improve their operations. The penalty which they charge on an early repayment of a loan is said to be excessive. I know a number of people who, because of the economic circumstances, have been forced to draw in their horns and liquidate some of their assets, with the idea that they could pay off some of their indebtedness. However, they found they were not able to do so because of the very heavy penalties imposed by the FBDB on the retirement of their loans. I understand the other side of the argument presented by the FBDB, that it itself has had to borrow money at high rates, but I am sure that some kind of accommodation could be worked out to allow the early retirement of loans without this penalty, or to allow loans to be rolled over more easily without the penalty provisions which presently exist. A lot of businessmen got themselves into trouble by borrowing money at the very high rates of interest which existed a year and even six months ago. Now because of the drop in the level of interest rates they would like to roll over those loans so that their payments are much reduced. To enable them to do that would be to their benefit.
The last comment I would like to make is one of a general nature. It is in respect of the relationship between banks and borrowers. If you are a large corporation which borrows hundreds of millions of dollars, or if you are a country or state which borrows hundreds of millions of dollars, or on occasion billions of dollars, it is pretty easy for you to negotiate with your bank. When you owe your bank that much money, it is in your power. We have seen cases in the recent past where countries in actuality, Sir, have defaulted. I know that that is a bad word to use and banks do not like any suggestion of "default" when moneys of that magnitude are involved.
Small Businesses Loans Act
However, for loans of that magnitude it has been relatively easy for the borrower and the lender to sit down together and re-negotiate a schedule for repayment. Bansk have had to do that. But when it comes to small business, that is not the case. The head office of the bank will issue a blanket policy, and each manager and each local loan officer will be obliged to put it into effect. There is not too often much of chance to renegotiate a repayment schedule, and the line of credit is very often unilaterally cut off. If the system can be improved-and I am not really suggesting legislation because the more burdensome regulation we put on both the borrowers and the lending institutions, the more difficulty there is in the long run. Any decrease in efficiency caused by legislation or regulations ends up ultimately in an increase in the price of a loan. There is no doubt about that. I am suggesting, however, there are many ways, especially in the more remote parts of Canada, where the relationship between small business borrowers and the banking institutions can be improved.
We look forward to the swift passage of this legislation because we on this side feel that even if it does not go far enough, it will, to a limited extent, help the small business sector of Canada, that very important small business sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 4) AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TERMINATION DATE FOR LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) (Mr. Rompkey) explained his reasons for tabling this Bill. This afternoon, for the benefit of Hon. Members, and through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to highlight the objectives and impact of the Small Businesses Loans Act, a measure that is being used more and more by small businesses.
The Small Businesses Loans Act was passed by the House in 1961, to make it easier for small businesses to obtain longer term financing. The Act, which provides guarantees against all losses for the lender, was initially intended to be effective for

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
three years only. There have been several extensions, however. The Act now in effect will expire next Thursday, on March 31, 1983.
Mr. Speaker, since 1961, many amendments to the Act have been made, and I shall mention some of the most important ones. In 1974, the maximum amount of the loan that may be outstanding to anyone firm rose from $25,000 to $50,000. In 1977, the maximum was increased to $75,000, and in 1980, to the present limit which is $100,000. In 1977, the maximum annual turnover allowed for a business to be eligible was increased from $1 million to $1,500,000, and finally, in 1978, the administration of the Act was entrusted to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the maximum interest rate chargeable was now based on the bank's prime or basic rate plus 1 per cent, more commonly referred to as prime plus one.
One of the most attractive aspects of the program is that loans are negotiated directly by the businessman or woman with the private sector lender. No prior authorization is required from the Government, since the latter only guarantees the loan. Today, loans to small businesses are made for the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, improvement or modernization of premises, purchase or construction of new premises and the purchase of land.
Loans are made in accordance with normal banking practice. They are fully guaranteed and are to be repaid over a period not exceeding ten years.
Mr. Speaker, as a program, the Small Businesses Loans Act has been favourably received both by borrowers and lenders, and its national impact is considerable. According to our statistics on geographical distribution which are fairly representative of the distribution recorded since the program came into effect, loans, expressed in percentages, break down as follows:
British Columbia: 20.5 per cent; the Prairies: 18.8 per cent; Ontario: 21.6 per cent; Quebec: 33.3 per cent; the Maritimes: 5.5 per cent, and the Northwest Territories and the Yukon: 0.3 per cent.
I would like to pause here, Mr. Speaker, and comment on statements made by the Minister responsible for Industry in the Quebec Government, who said that the Canadian Government never does anything for small businesses. I may refer Hon, Members to a statement the Minister made before a meeting of Provincial Ministers of Industry was held here in Ottawa. The Minister said, and he referred to a plan known at the time as the Biron Plan, he said in the National Assembly, and I quote:
The Biron Plan was established a year ago-
I am quoting from an article in Le Droit, dated February 19, 1983:
The Biron Plan was established a year ago, when the Federal Government refused to create a special program to help small- and medium-sized businesses. Today-"
-the article goes on-
-we can say that we have reached our objective," said Mr. Biron, who pointed out that his plan had helped over 500 businesses employing nearly 25,000 workers, and involved funding of over $100 million. Since then, Mr. Speaker, we have asked for the addresses of these 500 companies which received assistance under the so-called Biron plan and we are still waiting for replies.
As for the Quebec Minister of Industry, he always says that the Federal Government never does anything whether it concerns transport or agriculture; the various Quebec Ministers, also share this view. According to them, the Federal Government never does anything!
In this regard, I must say that we have to ask ourselves seriously what is the main purpose of the recent controversy about the NEED program, and I do hope that this program will not fail. Of course the Quebec Government will not recognize the efficacity of this program because according to them the Federal Government can never do anything good. The Quebec Government wants to control the funds provided by the Federal Government. It does not work that way. The Federal Government wanted it known that these were Federal funds really provided by all Canadians. But it is always the same, Mr. Speaker.
I am mentioning all this because it is extremely important for the Quebec people to realize that they have had enough of such statements. I would like to give another example. Hon. Members are aware that the Federal Government contributes to the building of low-cost housing everywhere in Quebec and in the other provinces. Why a supposedly responsible Government be fair and give credit where credit is due? Everywhere you go in the province, and especially in my constituency, it is the same. For instance, the other day I went through Val des Bois and saw a sign which said "Quebec Housing Corporation, low-cost residential construction" written in large letters, and underneath, in small print "with the co-operation of the Val des Bois municipality and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation". On Marengere Street in Pointe-Gatineau, there is similar sign on which the Quebec Housing Corporation is mentioned in large letters, followed by the words "with the cooperation of the City of Gatineau and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation" in small characters.
This should be pointed out to the Opposition Members because the little game that they play in Quebec is childish. Why not give its due to the Federal Government? On September 7-
