speechtext:
Yes, I was the one footing the bill. Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to emphasize this point: The Federal Government, through the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is participating in this project to the tune of $2,224,800 in guaranteed loans-$2.5 million makes a rounder figure-an amount which represents the total cost of the project. Moreover, the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation will provide on a continuing basis a subsidy of over $306,463 a year. The Canadian Government therefore pays between 72 and 75 per cent of the operational deficit at the end of the year-I should not say 75 when it is 72 perhaps, I would not want my separatist opponents to call me a liar- and the balance of 28 or 25 per cent is shared by the municipality of Gatineau and the Provincial Government.
I have not checked this with my Quebec colleagues, but here the story is always the same with respect to signboards: the name of the Societe d'habitation du Quebec appears in 6- or 8-inch high letters, and "with the participation of the town of Gatineau and the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation" is acknowledged in letters measuring about three quarters of an inch, maybe an inch. Why? It is the same thing on our buildings where people have to go, not to beg but to get social benefits because they have been hard hit by the current recession. The flag of Quebec is displayed, but the fact is that the benefits handed out by that department are paid at the rate of 50 per cent by the Federal Government and 50 per cent by the province, be it Ontario, Manitoba or any other. Unfortunately, Quebec will not admit that the Federal Government pays its share.
Small Businesses Loans Act
Perhaps I am slightly out of order when I say that, but my point is that when Industry Minister Biron comes along and states that he has spent so many dollars to help small businesses, I would advise the people of Quebec to check before quoting those statements, because sometimes they are halftruths. I would not say that the Minister is telling lies, but he does get carried away now and then and he does not always speak the truth.
Well, Mr. Speaker, back to the piece of legislation we want to adopt today. Besides being available in all regions of Canada, the program has enabled the Government to give assistance to a wide range of businesses. According to the 1982 figures, the service industries got 40.3 per cent of the total amount of loans, followed by retail outlets with 24.9 per cent, manufacturing companies with 11.4 per cent, construction firms with 9.4 per cent, and transport companies with 9.8 per cent. Other companies in the communications and wholesale sectors received 4.2 per cent of the loans.
At first, only chartered banks were allowed to act as lenders under the program. Over the years, the program was extended to other lenders, and today, in addition to banks, the list includes trust companies, mortgage companies and savings banks, while hundreds of credit unions, caisses populaires and branches of the Alberta credit union network also make loans. The number and amount of the loans contracted in 1981 and 1982 demonstrate how important the program is to small businesses, whatever Minister Biron, the Separatist Minister of Industry in the Quebec Government may have to say about it. In 1977, only 4,894 loans representing a total amount of $96 million were granted. In 1981, the number of loans had risen to 17,378 and totalled $516 million, while the preliminary figures for 1982 are almost identical, namely, 16,843 loans representing a somewhat smaller amount, namely, $435 million. These figures are ample proof of the importance of the Bill we are considering in the House today.
I would like to end on this note, Mr. Speaker, because otherwise I would be tempted to make a few more references to Mr. Biron, but I think he has had enough attention for today. Nevertheless, it is very sad to see someone from my own Province trying to sell the people a bill of goods. In any case, as far as small businesses are concerned, I heard my good friend from up North-I am not too sure what his constituency is-saying that we should not forget small businesses. Well, I do not think we are forgetting them today, and we have wanted to pass this Bill for a long time. Therefore, I hope that my colleagues opposite will do their share to show Canadians that this Bill is really going to help them, and I would also invite the Members of the New Democratic Party to vote for all stages of the Bill this afternoon, so that we will be able to tell Canadians that the Act is not going to expire on March 31 but will be extended for another two years.

March 25, 1983

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 4) AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TERMINATION DATE FOR LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-144, an Act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act. The effect of this will be to extend the termination date for loans to be guaranteed from March 31, 1983 to March 31, 1985. I hope that this will assist small business. Today, they have a great problem with red tape and trying to obtain loans from the banks.
The Government could help small business in the Province of Manitoba which is not receiving its fair share of public works expenditures. That is why I am pressing the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to build a new air traffic control centre in Winnipeg. In 1982, Manitoba received only $4 million public works grants. I hope the Minister will make an early appearance before the Treasury Board to request funding so that construction can be started on the air traffic control centre so that 250 air traffic controllers and their families will not have to move away from Winnipeg.
I am glad that the Minister is in the House this afternoon. I hope he can provide me with an answer before three o'clock, as he promised in Question Period, as to when construction will start. He complained that I did not give him notice of questions. Mr. Speaker, I did give notice last week to his Parliamentary Secretary in the adjournment debate. It would appear that he did not get the message. I hope I hear from the Minister before three o'clock on when construction of the new air traffic control centre in Winnipeg will begin.
I want to deal with the difficulties that small businesses have in obtaining loans in Manitoba. It is not only Government red tape and regulation that hampers them but they also experience great difficulty in obtaining help from banks.
A constituent who had applied for a small business loan wrote to me as follows:
I spoke several times with our bank-Toronto Dominion. They refused on the grounds that we are financially not stable enough.
Then I requested to get the Government bond for small business from our bank. They refused on the grounds that we are financially not weak enough to qualify.
I spoke several times with the Federal Development Bank about obtaining an interest break on a loan to help set up the food store. They refused on the grounds that we had purchased used equipment. In order to qualify we would have to have bought new equipment.
I hope the Government will change that ridiculous regulation.
It was only because we were able to purchase good used equipment that we were able to get the food store going, new equipment was just out of our reach.
That is a roadblock that the Government places in the way of this small businessman and probably of others in Canada. He went on:
I also went to the Economic Department of Manitoba. There they refused on the grounds that we did not start operating before June, 1981.
That is a New Democratic Party Government which is supposed to assist small business, but it is throwing up roadblocks here as well; it has imposed a worker's tax on Manitoba businesses which hampers them. With that regressive NDP tax many small businesses have to lay people off. It can be described as an anti-employment tax. It will not help with the unemployment problem. This gentleman went on to say:
As you see I did not get anywhere with all my inquiries. Your help would be much appreciated since time is running out.
To set up the food store I had to take out two second mortgages of $28,000 each at interest rates of 5 per cent above prime. Then a $25,000 loan with the Federal Development Bank at 4.5 per cent above prime. At present I have to take out a mortgage on our cottage of $37,000 at 12.25 per cent. At this rate it is hard to survive.
It is hard to believe that he did not just throw in the sponge and give up. With these regulations and the problems with the banks, it is almost impossible for small business to survive in Canada today.
In January, 1983, a newspaper put out by a small business called Mandate had an excellent article on the problems being experienced by Canadian experience. It stated that the average Canadian bank manager has less and less time available to service small business clients because of the literally hundreds of other bank services he or she must manage. It quoted Patricia Johnson, Vice-President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, as saying that excessive collateral requirements are used to paper over the fundamental structural problems in Canadian banking.
In some highlights the article pointed out that Canadian banks provide far less staff training in commercial lending than do banks in the United States, Japan or West Germany. It said that bank staff trainees in Japan call on business clients weekly to pick up deposits and loan payments, and if a business is facing difficulty, the bank may send in a rescue squad, at its own expense, to help the firm.
The article went on to say that two-thirds of U.S. banks have at least one officer designated for small business lending and about 40 per cent of there give special training to small business officers.
According to the article, in the Netherlands the largest small-business banks keeps credit officers in the same branch for a minimum of four years, maintaining continuity of service to small business clients. Canadian banks should provide the same service to Canadian small business, Mr. Speaker. The Government should show leadership in this area by having discussions with the banks to make sure that they improve their services and assist small business in Canada instead of sloughing them off.
On March 23, The Globe and Mail carried an article entitled "Survey depicts recession impact". The article began:
The economic impact of the recession on Canada's small and medium-sized businesses accounts for 700,000 to 800,000 fewer jobs, or nearly half the country's unemployed workers, according to a survey by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
March 25, 1983

Restraint measures-including layoffs, reduced wages and cuts in investment-have severely hampered the performance of the small business sector. A survey in February conducted by the 64,000-member organization revealed the extent of the recession on small and medium-sized businesses since January, 1981.
The 14,171 companies that responded were forced to cut employment by 42,470-which, if extrapolated to cover the entire small business community, means 700,000 to 800,000 fewer jobs across Canada.
You can see the difficulty that small business is having, Mr. Speaker. The banks and the Government will have to put their heads together to find new ways to assist small businesses, and not throw roadblocks in their paths.
Here is another example from one of my constituents in Winnipeg-Assiniboine. He points out:
We have been trying since early August to obtain our bank's approval for an interest-reduced loan. The Government Information Centre who we were referred to said 'Go to your bank manager.'
The problem is the banks have no information that authorizes them to give loans under this program.
That is unbelievable. We are here debating this small business Bill today and I feel that it will have very little impact in assisting small businesses in Canada. These Bills, Government advertising and bally-hoo sound great politically. The letter continues:
Sounds great politically-but how do we go about getting it from our bank?
Trust you will look into this on our behalf. My home is in your constituency.
I made representations on behalf of the gentleman. We were able to get some action taken for him. However, many small businesses must come to their Members' Parliament who then have to go after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister responsible for Small Businesses (Mr. Rompkey). This takes weeks of letter-writing, and in the meantime the small businessman is left to hang out to dry, waiting in anticipation.
I wish to cite for the record a number of problems that small businesses are facing. The Government has tried to raise revenue through measures that will hurt the small business community. The half-year convention will hurt the cash flow of business, and this is covered in a paper called "The Evolving Budget, A Background Paper on C-143".
The 12.5 per cent small business dividend distribution tax will punish those small businessmen who have dared to become successful enough to pay a dividend. You get more penalties if you make a profit.
The Small Business Development Bond has become a bailout bond with an interesting "catch 22" situation. People cannot apply unless they are in trouble and if they are in trouble, the bank will not lend them the money.
Small-businessmen will no longer be able to participate in new deferred profit-sharing plans. That is another penalty.
Increased taxes on employment benefits will place increased wage demands on employers and make it hard to recruit employees in remote areas. I have also referred to the NDP tax
Small Businesses Loans Act
in Manitoba, the employee tax, or perhaps unemployment tax would be better terminology.
With regard to skilled help, the recession has temporarily helped to resolve the shortage of skilled help, a problem often faced by small-businessmen. Steps should be taken now to ensure that recovery does not mean the return of skill shortages.
With respect to financing, the focus of recent Government policy has been to assist in debt financing. Assistance is needed but not forthcoming in the area of equity financing. The Government should encourage Canadians to invest in small business.
Another problem concerns regulation and paper burdens. Small businessmen are forced to comply with a complex series of regulations and requests from various Government agencies for statistical and other information. The owners of small businesses spend about half of their time filling out the most complicated and silly business forms and questionnaires imaginable. All this time they spend on those forms detracts from their business.
As well, in regard to the Government purchasing policy, Government contracts are far too often too large for most small businessmen to bid on, or the specifications may be written in such a way that only a few larger firms may meet the requirements.
We hope that the contents of this Bill will assist small businessmen, but there is much left to be desired in the way the banks are dealing with small business. There is too much Government regulation and red tape. I hope the Government and the banks will get together and eliminate many of these regulations and the red tape. I hope the Government will insist that the banks hire professional help to go out and assist small businesses to survive in Canada.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 4) AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TERMINATION DATE FOR LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill which is before us extends the period under which the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act will be available into the year 1985.
The Minister is taking the opportunity once again to extend the Small Businesses Loans Act which has, since January, 1961, provided the Government with an excuse to claim that it has done something, however little, for the small business sector in Canada.
Our Party does not intend to delay this Bill since the Government has indicated that to do so would be futile. It will not allow improvements to be made to the very weak provisions of this Bill. Its provisions were weak when the legislation was first proclaimed over 20 years ago. They have been made even less important as they have been seriously eroded by inflation.
The shortcomings of this and other Bills which are supposed to help small business have been well documented by organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. We believe that the Government's refusal to make improvements is perhaps more indicative than anything else of

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
the Government's attitude toward small business. It is obvious that the Government's view of small business is one of disdain, tokenism and, indeed, sheer lack of interest.
The fact of the matter is that the Government has not even considered amending this Bill in order to give the Small Businesses Loans Act some real impact. The Government says that it is deeply concerned about the economy. It has made much of its determination to cut the wages and salaries of workers in order to deal with inflation. However, why does the Government not increase the S100,000 loan limit which has been provided for in this Bill for a number of years when both the cost of living and the cost of doing business have increased very markedly? It is apparent that the Government is not prepared to move at all.
The Government says that it is concerned about the alarming rate of bankruptcies in the business community, which it should be. We have seen a string of Government bail-outs of the big corporations in this country, such as Dome Petroleum, Massey-Ferguson, Chrysler and others over the last year. But what has it done for the small business community, which makes up over 97 per cent of Canadian businesses? The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has estimated that in the last year 80,000 small businesses either went bankrupt or closed down before being forced into bankruptcy.
It would be relatively simple to reduce the bankruptcy rate of small businesses by extending the Small Businesses Loans Act to include loans for working capital, broadening the range and impact of this now very restrictive program and allowing thousands of small businessmen, who are now on the brink of bankruptcy as a result of the current depression and the Liberal Government's destructive interest rate policy, to obtain loans for badly needed working capital to keep people working. That was the type of proposal made by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and rejected completely by the Government.
The present legislation provides loans for the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, land for the operation of the business or the construction of new premises. But this can only be done up to the legislated limit of $100,000. Hon. Members need only to think of cities in their ridings to realize that it is difficult to find a single family home in many cities in Canada that does not cost at least $100,000.
Does the Government really expect a loan program which was established in 1961 and later extended to the upper loan limit of $100,000 to provide any real incentive to small businesses in 1983?
Another aspect of the program which I feel deserves the attention of the House is the prime role which banks play in deciding who gets loans. The reputation of the chartered banks of Canada for making huge loans to big corporations and then allowing those corporations to have interest-free holidays from those loans is well known. We know, for example, that in the last couple of years, the chartered banks lent billions of dollars to some of our largest corporations, mainly for takeovers of other corporations, takeovers which added little, if anything, to our productive capacity.
We know that a few months ago the banks were carrying $4.2 billion, or $4,200 million, in what they called nonproductive loans. Those were loans which large companies had made on which they could not even pay the interest, let alone the principal. However, these banks, the big five, increased their profits by over 40 per cent in the first quarter of this year. The total profits were $1.6 billion, on which they paid the magnificent tax of only $132 million. That is an average tax rate of just 8.1 per cent. Two of the banks, the Bank of Montreal and the Royal Bank, paid no tax at all in 1982. In fact, they received a tax credit. I wonder which of our constituents would not love to have a tax rate on their income of just 8 per cent.
At the same time the banks were dealing with the large corporations, as I have indicated, small businesses requesting loans were being asked to put up collateral of anywhere from 200 per cent or 300 per cent of the value of the loans. It is therefore no wonder that when the Canadian Federation of Independent Business appeared before the appropriate committee of the House of Commons, it made the statement that in its view, banks, as they operate today, do not understand the problems of small business and have very little sympathy for small business.
We say that when the Government puts programs such as this into place, there should be consideration for the possibility of going outside the banking system to deliver such programs in a more direct and clearly much more beneficial way to the small business sector. One must only consider the squeeze which the banks have put on the consumers and small business borrowers in order to carry the big corporate loans to see whom the banks are really interested in servicing.
In this country, we have a small business sector of over 600,000 private enterprises, yet to the end of 1981, the Small Businesses Loans Act had provided less than 100,000 loans, representing slightly less than $2 billion. That is in over 20 years. In comparison to that, the small business sector is estimated to borrow close to $9 billion a year from private sources, from the banks, the credit unions and insurance companies. Therefore, we see the over-all insignificance of the small businesses loans programs.
Big business in Canada is 48 per cent foreign-owned. The small business sector represents about 96 per cent of Canadian ownership and over 50 per cent of the private sector jobs which have been created since 1971. Small business provides 40 per cent to 50 per cent of all the jobs at which Canadians work outside of the public sector, yet the assistance that small business recieves from the Government is miniscule as compared to the help which big business routinely receives from the federal and provincial Governments. Small business deserves more than the highest bankruptcy rate since the depression which it has experienced in the last year.
We have some specific proposals as to what should be done instead of what will be done as a result of passage of the Bill. We believe that the $100,000 limit on the program should be increased to bring it more into line with the real cost of business start-ups and business operation in 1983. We believe
March 25, 1983

that the program should be broadened to reflect the need of small businesses for working capital to keep their operations, which are now hard-pressed because of the recession, going and to keep them out of bankruptcy which has been increasing in numbers over the last couple of years.
We believe that the delivery system for this program, which has been channeled through the chartered banks which, as intermediaries, have been sitting in judgment on small business loan decisions, should be reconsidered. Why should it not be possible to have a loans screening body in which small business would participate and have some say, rather than leaving it entirely to the banks which have failed so lamentably to meet the need of small business?

Members of the House, and it is timely for Canadians who are involved in small business. First, I think we must be a little careful concerning the words "small business". In fact, I had lunch with a "small businessman", in the words classified under the Act, just today. I was discussing with him, as a businessman, the advantages and disadvantages of his business at the present time. It is sometimes good to get back to the grass roots to find out what the very people who will be affected by legislation before the House are saying with regard to it. He is involved in a service industry in my riding. His first real comment concerned the definition of small business. The vast majority of those involved in small business, at least those in service industries in rural Canada, will argue that the definition is too broad and that at the upper end, in terms of size as set out in the definition of small business, in fact they are often not considered to nearly the degree they should be, in relation to the number of jobs they create in the economy.
It is also important that we as Members of the House keep in mind the impact of small business on our country. We discuss the unemployment rate and speak of one and a half million Canadians being unemployed. We hear those comments in the House, we consider the statistics, and we view the tragedy. Today in the House there were comments as to how we should create, or develop jobs. I think that "develop" is a more accurate word than "create". For instance, how are we to develop jobs for young people as they come on to the labour market?
How should we develop jobs so that these people will not face despair or, more important, feel as they enter the market that the economy will not give them the opportunity to either create their own jobs or to fit into the job market? It is important for us to address this matter in the debate today as well. However, it is important to keep in mind that the owners of businesses to whom we speak as we go into our ridings, the people on Main Street, Canada, the fellows with whom we
Small Businesses Loans Act
have coffee around the horseshoe, are people who can create jobs in our community. These are the small business people, and we all know them. We can give various names to these people, because they are friends, neighbours and are very often our community leaders.
We must keep in mind that in this period of unemployment, it is small business which is most often labour-intensive. Today, a number of small businesses, as they are facing the spring and summer of this year, are considering expansion of their businesses. As they do this, they automatically think of the creation of work, the hiring of people in their community. Small business is labour-intensive. Also, by all definition, we find that in small business there is a higher ratio of job creation relative to investment per job as compared to larger businesses. Therefore, it is a good use of money, a good investment. I am obviously trying to build the case that we in this House have not paid enough attention to these facts, to small business or, in my view, to the country.
Also, small business creates more opportunities for workers with limited skills. That does not say that they would not develop their skills in the workplace, but I am speaking of initial hirings. For example, very often small business is more ready to hire people with limited skills, and then develop those skills in the workplace, than larger industry is.
Today more than 90 per cent of our businesses in Canada are employing less than 200 people in their business. For a lot of us from rural Canada, a business of 200 employees is a fairly large business. We have some of those businesses in my riding, but a lot of us would welcome that kind of size in our riding.
I hear references made to anti-profits, anti-business, "We are going to get the corporate welfare bums and we are going to get all of these people". It is an attitude that I believe we have to change very dramatically.
I am not trying to be critical today but I am trying to analyze the situation to see how we can have some positive direction. Governments of all Parties put a great stress on the concept of megaprojects, be it energy or manufacturing, but especially in energy we have talked about megaprojects. The investment per job is very high. I am in favour of megaprojects; I am in favour of business; I am in favour of creation of wealth through that kind of investment, but I do not think Governments have given the same stress to smaller businesses and what they mean to the economy. For instance, how much time do we spend in this House discussing megaprojects? How much time do we spend in this House talking about small business? Yet if we say that 90 per cent of business is small business, I think we have to re-examine our priorities.
In our Canadian economy, the economic engine is small business, and I include farming in small business. The reason I put farming into that category is that I speak to farmers in my

constituency and they are business people with a myriad of skills, not only in farming. Today if a farmer wants to survive he also has to have business acumen second to none, equal to the person operating on Main Street, Canada. I put them in that category as well.
I have been interested for some time in the psychological relationship between business and financial institutions, and maybe that is a topic that does not excite the House too much, but I think it is important for us to analyze what other countries have done relative to business, and what we have done and why. Maybe there are some answers in other countries that we could apply to help the economy in Canada.
When I make these points about other countries I am not saying that other countries have these motivations exclusively and that Canada has none of them. I am strictly talking about stress and emphasis. But there is no doubt that in the United States there has been a great emphasis on the spirit of enterprise. Some people would say "free enterprise", some people would say "the market economy". Teenagers today use the term "Go for it". I think that term possibly explains that attitude, that spirit of going for it, having the confidence, being willing to take the risk, going for it and enjoying the benefits of success. I guess that is what enterprise means; that is the modern term.
There has been a great reverence in the United States for the common person, a reverence for that drive that I have already talked about and a reverence for the contribution of the individual to the larger whole. When I say that, I do not mean that we in Canada are devoid of that. I am not arguing that point. I am simply talking about emphasis of that point.
So when I look at Government agencies in the United States, despite the fact that so often we talk about economies of scale of ten to one, United States to Canada, I find a very deep interest and a stress in U.S. Government circles on small business. So what is happening? As I look at it there, for instance, I see they have created a banking system quite different from ours. I am not here today to criticize the banks. I know that is a common and easy hobby-horse, but I want to look very specifically at why there is that difference. One thing I notice in their system is that they have a different banking mix than we have. They have different banking services. The percentages of national or large banks, that is, relative to the amount of deposits, is lower in the United States than it is in Canada, compared with our national chartered banks. They have many more local banks. They might call them savings and trusts, but they are local banks. I know the first argument that I am going to get is that it is too risky. But that is the secret of enterprise, taking risks, not unqualified risks but taking risks.

It is competition, and I am not saying that it need be a credit union, it could be a savings and loans company or a trust company, but the competitive nature of the financial marketplace has the same laws as enterprise in other business. That is the point I am trying to get across.
Looking at the United States, we find that the larger commercial banks, and for our purposes here today we could compare them to our national chartered banks, instead of 74 per cent, are down to about 57.5 per cent or 58 per cent. But also, their banks are more commercially oriented, not in all cases, but I believe the majority lean more toward the commercial end of banking. Some people would argue that, with the economies of scale in the United States, obviously that is larger business. The only point I am trying to make today is that according to the psychology that we have developed in our own country it would appear to me that we have possibly erred on the side of safety as against the willingness to take risks.
When we look at loans for small business in Canada, we make the case strongly that loans are made on the basis of what is referred to as formula lending. In other words, when a businessman or woman goes into the banking institution to ask for a loan, first there are the standard questions of collateral investment. When speaking to some business people, they say they would sure like to get their hands on the little black book from which decisions are often made. These decisions are often not made at the branch level. In the national banking system there is a much larger network of branches, depending of course on the district or the central bank.

While we cannot forget about formula lending, I suggest the banks would be well advised to re-examine some of their mix. I believe their profitability could be increased by greater involvement in small business. It seems to vary from branch to branch. There are branches in my riding that are excellent in commercial activity and small business. The local branch manager has experience, expertise and the confidence of the local business community. It is a secret that we must look at. On balance, our banking system serves well, but I hope it will look at the mix, the balance, more carefully when considering small business.
Having said that, what about Government? How is Government helping small business? The arguments about Government, the lack of interest and the disincentives towards small business are legendary. We hear about them every day in this House.
Earlier today the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) talked about Manitoba. Right now approximately 37 per cent of Manitoba's total budget is federal-provincial transfer payments, and it is going up. One of the great advantages in that Province has always been relatively low-priced electrical energy, hydraulic energy. There was a freeze on hydro-electric increases. Why? When you have one million people in a given region, you must give a reason why a business should establish there rather than somewhere else where there is a larger population. When you take away the incentive of stable and competitive prices for energy, then the reasons of distance and space become more important in the decision-making process. I say let us look at good loan programs; they are much better. 1 suggest we have competitive loan programs which allow for profitability and expansion rather than all kinds of grants which result in paper work, questions and disincentives.

The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) comes from the business world, and I respect that, but why is he getting public servants involved in running businesses and providing incentives? The Government can give $34 million to Maislin, but cannot consider giving a $250,000 guaranteed loan to small business in this country.

The record shows, Mr. Speaker, that these loans have been very successful. The cost has been minimal to the Government, and what a bonanza it would be today to create jobs.
Government has gone into research and development on a hit and miss basis. It has no programs. If they hear something one day they go into it. There is no total, global program for these people. Then we have the miscellaneous Government grab bags. There are so many I cannot keep track and I do not know how industry does. The Government does it this way: there are consultants in Ottawa to whom you go to find out where you can get your money. That, to me, is an economic waste. Surely one solid industry and trade program can be set down, one simple program. Let us not talk about $100,000 for this one and $500,000 for that one. Let us go big and think big. Let us start perhaps at between $2 million and $5 million maximum, because that is what you need today. You need much larger sums of money because industry is that much more capital intensive.
When we give this money, we should not, as a Government, have to guarantee 100 per cent of these loans. We should process them entirely through the banks and let the banks accept 50 per cent of the risk. They make the profits. Why should they not accept a portion of the risk? If that is done, it could be very effective for a new corporation or a new expansion by reducing the interest rate until the building is built and the turnover is at a level where the industry can afford to start repaying interest. What has happened in this country, Mr. Speaker, is that we have capitalized interest to the point where we are no longer competitive.
I am very concerned about that when I look at the international competition we must deal with. There are many examples right in my riding. I received a phone call last week from a company by the name of Whitby Welding. It is a very old, well-recognized and established company which exported over 50 per cent of its products. That company is being put on the ropes by the bank because during the high interest period when it had growth, the company kept paying these interest amounts out, and when sales dropped off because of lack of demand, they had already built up the cost by building up the plant and its equipment. But they still have the interst rates to contend with. If there was a flexible interest rate policy where interest rates would go up and down depending on the economy, we could pay for the subsidized interest rates very simply out of saved Unemployment Insurance benefits and welfare benefits. Furthermore, and this is something that is really close to me, the people would feel better about themselves if they were employed rather than sitting at home drinking beer. This is the key.
To go back to Whitby Welding, if they would have had a fixed low rate of interest, or a flexible rate of interest, they could have survived, but the bank not only pushed them for the interest, they demanded repayment of all their loans. I have not heard from this company in the last week, but I hope they found some relief through Industry, Trade and Commerce,
because they are a fine company. They are wonderful men who run it, and they are very good supporters of mine, I must admit. Furthermore, the president happens to be one of my major fund raisers, and I really need him back on track. But, you see, Mr. Speaker, that is what we represent. This Party represents small industry and those people get behind us because they believe in free enterprise, freedom of ownership and the individual.
We are letting this country down, Mr. Speaker, because of our policies. We are not being fair to the people. We are saying that unions are no good instead of trying to encourage cooperation between Government, the employer and labour, giving some form of incentive for productivity. We are not looking in that direction.
Let us look at what other countries have done so successfully. I have great admiration for Japan but, Mr. Speaker, you have heard me in my place argue against letting any more cars into this country from Japan because it is going to hurt employment in my area. The Government has not given any incentive to our producers to change over to high technology. However, in Japan a small-businessman can lease from the Japanese Government one or two robots. He does not pay any rental on those robots until he perfects the process. Then he leases them on a long-term scheme at an increasing scale so that he can afford to become more productive in his industry.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-144 has been discussed at length in some detail but perhaps it would be useful if I put on the record for those who will be following this debate at home the history of the Bill.
The Small Businesses Loans Act has been around for some years. Originally it was introduced in 1961. One of the fascinating parts of the Bill before us today is that when it was last before us for amendment in 1981 the loan ceiling was raised from $850 million to $1.5 billion, being the maximum outstanding debt covered by the Act. It is ironic that in this year of 1983, when we are asked to extend the life of this Bill from the middle of 1983 to the middle of 1985, the Government has not contemplated it being necessary to increase that ceiling. I honestly do not know why there has not been an increase. I suspect that the reason there is not an increase is that Government Members opposite, and I am sure the departmental officials, know that what is likely to happen in the next couple of years is that people who qualify for these loans, new businesses or businesses increasing are expanding their operations-I note in passing that debt restructuring or the consolidation of existing debt is particularly not allowed under the SBLA-those people are not likely very many.
That is the tragedy of the recession we are in. There were some figures in the business section of The Globe and Mail yesterday which indicated the views of businesses in Canada as to their potential for expansion and new spending or even getting back to where they were before the recession began. While I do not have the figures with me, if my memory serves me very few businesses in Canada of any size, small, medium or large, foresee that they will be increasing their capacity. Very few businesses are likely to undertake expansion programs over the next few years. That is understandable, if sad,

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
if you simply look at the crisis of confidence which I find, at least in my area of Toronto, the majority of businessmen feel about this country.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I come back to the original point: it is not surprising that the Bill to extend the life of the borrowing guarantee does not at the same time increase the maximum capacity of the borrowing guarantee. That reflects, I believe, a recognition that there is unlikely to be a good deal of borrowing.
A number of Members today have put on the record, Mr. Speaker, their concerns about small business. My chief reason for rising is to add my few comments to that debate. There is not a Member in this Elouse who does not have a very substantial small business community in his riding. Therefore, it is, I am sure, one of the areas of debate common to all of us. There is no reason or necessity to be partisan on this question. I do not think there is a Member in this House who is not experiencing every day and every month the misery of bankruptcy in his home town or community on the part of dozens of people and dozens of businesses. There would be no point trying to make partisan points on an issue such as that.
Perhaps Hon. Members opposite will understand that some of us are trying to encourage the Government to recognize that the small business programs it has in place today are really just ways of further bandaging the wounded in the hope that they will some day be able to get back into the economic war. It is really not meant in a partisan manner. It is a plea to recognize the general thrust of Government policy on the small business community at a time when that community has never been more needed by the Canadian economy.
Some of us have been pleading since the beginning of this session for some relief on the mortgage interest question. Members opposite have pooh-poohed it, but it is particularly appropriate in today's discussions because the largest small business sector is the construction sector. While small businesses comprise about 24 per cent of Canadian industry, in the construction sector small businesses make up 55 per cent of it.
When other Hon. Members and I raise this issue, we raise it precisely in the context of what the Government could do to get the construction industry going without a great deal of cost to Government at a time when unemployment in that industry is 35 per cent. Also companies simply cannot use a vehicle such as the one before us today because they are not in a position to invest in new plant or equipment since no business is being done and there is no real prospect of a great deal of new housing construction. speechtext:
I appreciate and accept the recommendation of the Hon. Member. I am careful when quoting from any newspaper, particularly this one. I appreciate that my comments may not be directly on Bill C-144, but I think they come
March 25, 1983

much closer to the rules of relevancy than some of the other aberrations which have taken place. The article reads in part:
The Act's main drawbacks are that secured creditors and landlords now have powers that can actively prevent a reorganization. Also, preferred creditors including Governments and employees-whose claims rank behind those of secured creditors and ahead of unsecured creditors-must be paid immediately if reorganization takes place.
That point is critically important, because the article refers to a small business which at the time was trying to reorganize itself in order to avoid bankruptcy and obtain a chance to get back into the ranks of profitable companies, presumably to be able some day to take advantage of the legislation which is before us today.
I return momentarily to my first comment, that this is at least as important an issue as the legislation before us today which itself, by not raising the limit, recognizes that there are not likely to be a great number of applications for that form of relief.
The article continues:
In the case of Hi-Fi Express, several creditors had asked Price Waterhouse to create a debt restructuring proposal .. . But it was not possible because of potential trouble with landlords . .. and because Government debts totalled at least $250,000.
Now, $250,000 to a big business is not a lot of money. To a small business it is an incredible amount of money. To a business which spends $87 billion per year, called the Government of Canada, it is a tiny, tiny drop in the bucket. Therefore, the effect of that legislation is that the Government of Canada is itself the reason a business going bankrupt cannot be restructured to try and survive. I literally did not know that. In fact I am quite stunned that we would be dealing with other legislation rather than resolving that issue. There is no question that the extension before us today is important. As little good as it will do, at least it will do something.
I was astounded yesterday when I read the suggestion that the other Bill, in layman's language, could have a tremendous impact. I am referring to that one item alone, not necessarily the entire Bill. When the Government is owed tax, it should recognize that it would be wiser to avoid putting people on the unemployment and welfare rolls and simply postpone the debt in a re-arranged structure to give the owners and employees the right to continue working and a chance to pay the debt rather than put them out of business.
It amazes me that that legislation has not yet been before the House, at a time when the issue is not as much finding new sources of borrowing money for small business as helping them restructure. When I was thinking about some comments to make in today's debate, I was a little perplexed to discover that the Government has been sitting on a piece of legislation which I think my small businesses need more than the legislation before the House. If anything, small businesses need both, yet the Government's priority over debt restructuring legislation and amendments to the Bankruptcy Act is the sports pool or lottery Bill to help fund a very important event, the Calgary Olympics due to take place in 1988. That has a higher priority today for the Government of Canada than amendments that
Small Businesses Loans Act
would help small business to survive. I think you will understand, Mr. Speaker, if I find that more than moderately astounding.
When we are dealing with this question it seems more appropriate to ask the Government to remove whatever the roadblock is on that particular provision of that legislation and allow us to deal with it as expeditiously as we have agreed to deal with the two items that are before the House today. 1 do not believe that any Member of the Government has fewer problems in his small business constituency than a Member on this side of the House. I appeal to Hon. Members opposite to move at least that piece of legislation forward as quickly as possible. I do not think they want to see any small business go into bankruptcy if there is a way to prevent it. To find that the Government is an agency that is creating bankruptcy is terrifying in these times.
One could speak at great length about other dilemmas but I want to put on record one small matter, Mr. Speaker, and that is the 12.5 per cent tax on small business dividends paid to shareholders and owners. This is a technical matter for most Canadians who do not receive dividends. The Government's proposals on that matter have excited more comment from owners and operators of small business in my constituency than any other in the budget, however. It would be inappropriate if I did not take this opportunity to register their concerns.
Finally, I should like to say to the Government that its willingness to bring the legislation forward at this time and have it go through is to be commended.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 4) AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TERMINATION DATE FOR LOANS
speechtext:
That is the largest round of applause that has occurred in the House all day, Mr. Speaker, and it is an indication of the interest there is in this debate.
It is an important debate, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about the segment of the business community that is being hurt very badly. The Hon. Member for Don Valley West, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) have spoken about the problems that they face in their constituencies. I am sure you share those problems in your constituency and I know that the Minister of Transport shares them in his. We all know that there is no part of the business community that is hurting more than small business. We understand that from our mail and we understand it from the visits we make to the premises of small businesses in our constituency from time to time. The Hon. Member from Provencher spoke of instances in his riding.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, as could every Member of the House, but I think it is important that the debate be concluded today so I shall not take up the time of the House. I do not want it to be said, however, that because a problem is left unspoken, the problem is not an important one.
In my constituency I attended a meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In Canada, agriculture has been one of the most stable of small businesses but last year the rate of bankruptcy had increased 65 per cent over the previous year. That is a startling phenomenon, Mr. Speaker.
Although there are many doubts about what the House achieved with the Private Member's Bill to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangements Act introduced by the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson)-and which the Government had to be shamed into moving-there is no doubt in the agriculture sector of the business community that something has to be done.
As a result of passage of this Bill, amending the Small Businesses Loans Act, the ceiling for the period which has been extended from March 31, 1983 to March 31, 1985 for loans that can be guaranteed will be $1.5 billion. I share the view of the Hon. Member for Don Valley West that the ceiling is probably too low, just as the ceiling on the Farm Credit Act is too low. There is a crisis in agriculture, Mr. Speaker.
I do not mean to be partisan. For example, I do not believe that there is any room for crass partisanship in relationship to the economy. With the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson), Mr. Speaker, you and I attended a meeting in Toronto of the Canadian Construction Association attended by representatives of companies large and small in the construction business. These businesses operate in the constituencies of every Member of the House. Those people spoke of their situation with despair.
This Bill allows the rate of loans for small businesses to continue. In some manner it compensates for what I am sorry to say is the foolishness of the budgetary policy of the Government. To that extent it is supportable.
Close to half of all Canadians presently unemployed were formerly employed by small and medium-sized businesses. That is what The Globe and Mail reported today. They
represent close to half of the unemployed in Canada. In February, there were 1,585,000 people unemployed in Canada. According to the same report, the small business sector employs between 700,000 and 800,000 fewer Canadians than it did in January of 1981. That is a sad statistic. There is no place for partisanship when dealing with these statistics.
The other aspect dealt with in this same report is that few of these industries that were surveyed in this large survey that was conducted by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business have any plans to increase either hiring or investment. Of those industries surveyed, 66.7 per cent expect to retain present employment levels. Those are levels which have fallen off by almost a million from a year and a half ago. The fact that 9.1 per cent would be rehiring laid-off workers shows just how small the prospect for advancement is as we deal with this matter. Only 7.9 per cent will be hiring additional people. What impact will those little glimmers of optimism have on the 1,585,000 unemployed, half of whom were employed in small business? Is it any wonder that this Bill is important and we want to pass it tonight? I do not think so.
What reason did those surveyed give for this happening? They admitted that the recession is world-wide, a fact with which we are all aware. They say that much of the cause has been the result of a combination of damaging federal policies and intergovernmental bickering.
I would like to stop there for a moment and talk about damaging federal policy. There is no Member over there who is unhappy to see the MacEachen budget gutted piece by piece by the former Minister of Finance himself, who brought it in, and then the final crowning insult, swift and merciful death at the hands of the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). No one was unhappy about that. The Hon. Member for Gatineau was overjoyed to see it gutted. It cut the mail from his constituents by over 85 per cent.
Something which has characterized the national life of Canada and which I believe has been damaging not only to the country but to the sense of national will to achieve goals is the fact that there has been bickering among the Governments in Canada. In a federal state, co-operation, consultation, consensus, understanding and compromise are the catch words. Cooperation is essential whether we are applying it to how we treat the native people of Canada and deal with those problems, whether we are talking about an assault on the problems of agriculture or the environment, whether we are talking about transportation or attacking the problems of big business and the challenges facing the country. Co-operation is possible because we have co-operated before.
Last night, I met a man at the Infotech Display at the Sportsplex in my riding, which is an exhibition giving a view into the future of the computer and micro-technology industry in the National Capital area. He reminded me and the group I was with of this national will that we talk about. He reminded us that Canadians had a purpose during the war. We had a job
March 25, 1983

and the will to achieve something. We built airfields within a period of time that no one thought possible. We built airplanes at a rate at which no one said it could be done. We built ships, hangars and other installations.
I say to those people who are pessimistic about the country and feel that it is drifting with no hope that there is hope. In all the dismay and despair over the economic situation we are facing today, there is a challenge. It is the challenge of creating the national will. It is a challenge in which the Government must take the lead but, I am sorry to say, it has not done so. I do not say that in any partisan way. I suppose we are all to blame in one way or another. Government, in the broad sense, is to blame.
The battle which exists between labour and business in this country has been caused by an adversarial atmosphere. It is an atmosphere we will have to change because our competitors are changing. If there is new technology, we will either have to buy it or develop it because our competitors are buying it and developing it.
I believe that this country is capable of doing anything it sets its mind to. We are told of the riches and resources of our country. Of course we have riches and resources. We are fortunate never to have been scarred by war. We have never had to rebuild an institution. We have never had to rebuild a major transportation facility.
We are rich in something else. We are rich in talented people because we have one of the highest educational levels in the world. This is another challenge that we must face in the future. What will we say to those young people, some of whom are in school because they cannot get a job, when they graduate? What will we tell them if we have not taken up the challenge of creating a better atmosphere for them as they look to careers?
The new technology developing right here in the National Capital area shows promise for expansion not just in this area but in the country. Expansion is not only possible for that industry but new industries as well. When will we recognize the fact that it is a growth industry which has potential and one which cries out for investment capital? In order for that investment capital to come forward, a certain atmosphere and climate is required which the Government can set. That industry has told the Government what it needs, and I need not repeat it. The way out of the despair is by taking up the challenge.
There are many things which can be done with respect to that challenge. If anyone does not believe that there is a challenge to the country, let them know that an average of 40 Canadian businesses went bankrupt every working day last year. When the dust of those bankruptcies has settled, those firms will show debts totalling $2.3 billion. Let the Government consider figures like that if it is concerned about its revenues. Figures now indicate that the jobless rate in Canada is perhaps 20 per cent. If there was ever a time for us to emphasize our efforts on small and medium-sized businesses, it is now because it is an historical fact that the greatest sector to
Small Businesses Loans Act
play a part in creating jobs has been the small business sector. That is where the jobs are created.
My speech today is likely the last one I will make on an economic matter prior to a budget since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced today that he will shortly bring in his budget. I want the Minister of Finance to consider that evidence. I am sure that he will. I want the Minister of Finance to know that in terms of the position in which the country finds itself and what must be done about it, I do not believe there is crass partisanship. There may be differences, but there is no crass partisanship. There is no Canadian on either side of this House of Commons who does not want success from the budget and from economic policy. There is no Member of Parliament who relishes the thought, for whatever reason, of row upon row, line upon line, day after day, with his or her office being filled with young people who cannot get work and small business people who are worried.
I believe, as we were told at the Construction Association meeting in Toronto, that it is important to the country that the right answers be found by the Minister of Finance, that the right balance be struck by him, so that we do not destroy the battle against inflation which has been fought with a singleminded purpose, to the extent that small business has been ground into the ground, as well as the manufacturing sector. We do not want to forget the importance of that. However, we equally must not forget that, aside from the statistics on joblessness, we have a social problem. It is for that reason, because the Bill assists in that important sector, that we intend to support the Bill and allow it to go through today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether all of the interest expressed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), has shown how the crowds have rushed the other way. Certainly Hon. Members have debated the Bill on two Friday afternoons. As I start my remarks, the debate has been going on for five hours. What is it about this Bill which requires five hours at second reading? Yet it is of importance. I am astounded that besides the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey), only the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) has spoken from the Government side. They profess to be greatly interested in the operations of small business, and they know that Hon. Members, particularly those from the Province of Quebec-
[ Translation]
-particularly in Quebec, where the small business sector is the pivot of economic development, but in view of the lack of participation by Quebec Members, 1 wonder how interested they really are in this instrument which has proven so effective in the past to finance small businesses. After all, the figures which the Hon. Minister has tabled give us a good idea about the number of small businesses in Canada and their quality. A business may include only two persons. It may also include about 50 employees working for a family business. Because of

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
this, there is not a single village or small community in Quebec or elsewhere in the country where there are no small businesses. The lack of interest shown by the Quebec Members is therefore surprising. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, and this is even more surprising, when we examined Bill C-139 to amend the Income Tax Act, the Government Members remained completely silent and accepted a 12.5 per cent tax increase on the distribution of small business profits. It is right here in Bill C-139!

Why is that torpedo included in the Bill? It is part of the Government philosophy, demonstrated by the Minister of Finance who, in his budget of November 12, 1981 said: "We will increase the tax on small business dividends by 12.5 per cent. That will raise the taxes of the owner of the small business to about that of a salaried employee." In other words, the owner of the small business receives nothing for his worry, for putting up the money, for having to meet payrolls. For all of the responsibilities of running a business, he gets absolutely zilch. That is what the Government considers shall be the reward of running a small business. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a shame. I know that our friends over in the New Democratic Party talk long and loud about small business, but as soon as the word "profit" is mentioned-
[ Translation]
As soon as we speak about the profits or the profitability of a business-

-they jump on it with both feet as being quite immoral that anyone should make a profit out of business, particularly their love of soaking it to corporate profits.
As I said, corporate profits can be a partnership of two men or women or a combination, or a few individuals who have "Ltd," or "Inc." behind the name of their business. Their profits are considered to be immoral. But surely to goodness, is it not a cliche merely to say that small business cannot get on without profits? There must be profitability in order to pay the owner or owners their return, because they, too, are entitled to a fair return for their labours and worries.
This Bill extends by one year a form of loan operation with the chartered banks and other credit-granting institutions. We have heard lot of nonsense about the chartered banks neglecting small business. The reason I am speaking this afternoon is that I am primarily interested in the operations of the chartered banks, trust companies and other financial institutions in this country.
I recall last year when the Finance Committee, following a motion of this House that bank profits be examined, had before it as witnesses representatives of all of the major chartered banks, some of the trust companies and some other organizations. I recall the words of Rowland Frazee, the President and Chief Executive Officer of the Royal Bank,
which is Canada's largest bank. Mr. Frazee was able to show indisputably that the major portion of that bank's business is with small business. Small business is not just 15 or 20 accounts, but tens of thousands of accounts where financing is required.
We have seen high interest rates, the recession and the National Energy Program. In my Province, Mr. Speaker, how that Program caused small business to take it in the neck, across the back, across the knees and stomped on both feet. That was the result of the immediate and then cumulative effect of the National Energy Program. My colleagues from Saskatchewan, many of them whose constituencies are in oil-producing areas, saw the same thing happen.
Those businesses were the type of businesses that one just loved to see. It was hard work, it was risky, but the men and women involved were quite prepared to go out on the limb for heavy equipment for a few dollars down and hundreds of thousands of dollars of financing, and they made it pay. We saw population move to the western Provinces to participate in this economic boom. Certainly there were some large corporate entities that were there. They always have to be there, but the big bulk of the service industry, the drilling, the pipelaying, the road building, the list of jobs and types of operations are legion. That was all small business.
Then the plague hit, and what a sorry picture it has left. And we wonder why. The rest of Canada has suffered doubly from that. Ontario industry, machines, equipment, the steel industry, the automobile manufacturers, who lost tens of thousands of vehicles per year, all as a result of those dark days of 1981. Now we are trying to pick up the pieces.
Hopefully with a changed picture for the banks, since they will be able to use the Small Business Development Bonds, we have to give these people an opportunity to finance. No one has the cash. They cannot be expected to have the cash, and when their profit margins have been trimmed, there are no reserves. There are no socks or no bundles of money tucked under mattresses. We have to see that the legislation is available for those who want to act.
I do not want to see grants, because they become conditional, so give them incentives either by lower term loans or some incentives through the Income Tax Act so that those who want to do may do, those want to shake may shake, and we will get that fundamental, basic industry that is represented by all facets of small business back in motion.
Then we will see the ranks of the unemployed go down, not by make-work programs through the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). They will not deal with unemployment. We need small business to get back on its feet and employ those hundreds of thousands; in fact, there are well over a million people employed in small business.
For that reason, I hope that we would now be able to agree to this Bill going to Committee for Clause by Clause study. That should not be long, and then we will take the report stage.
March 25, 1983

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 4) AMENDMENT TO EXTEND TERMINATION DATE FOR LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate. 1 do not know what has happened since the Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) spoke, but the Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has spoken as well as the Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and I find myself virtually alone. I do not think 1 will change that either way, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-144 may have had adequate discussion but it certainly has not had lengthy discussion in the House. We heard from the Government benches a week or so ago that they wished this Bill to be passed in one day, passed immediately. I could understand that if this Bill to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act were Bill C-44, but when it is Bill C-144 I do not think that shows a great deal of urgency on the part of the Government.
It is a Bill that will extend something that is used, hopefully, by a lot of small businesses in Canada, by enterprisers and people who wish to contribute to the economy of Canada, hire fellow Canadians, expand and do what we all hope can be done in this country, which is to provide a better country to live in, a country in which people are not left without the dignity of employment, especially when we have over two million people in Canada right now who are left without the dignity that I know they want and that we have expressed to the Government that they want.
This Bill basically extends its life for another two years, and we endorse that. It has attached to it a consultative committee that is to advise the Minister as to what small businesses should be able to apply for loans and what small businesses should be allowed to accept loans. This committee is made up of members of small businesses and members of the financial community.
The imbalance that we have now in debt equity in small firms is very apparent to all Members who have consulted with firms in their constituencies and have kept an eye on the state of the economy in Canada over the last number of years. When the small business consultative committee makes its report, I would be very interested in seeing it tabled and made available as soon as possible to the Members of this House and the small business community throughout Canada.
Small Businesses Loans Act
The largest contributor to employment in this country is small business. There are over 645,000 small businesses in Canada. They employ 42 per cent of the work force and make up 25 per cent of our GNP. The enterprise spirit of these risk-takers provides productivity to our economy.
In 1982 there were close to 150,000 business start-ups. Unfortunately there have been some failures. Those people have the enterprise, spirit and will to risk their life savings and in many cases the life savings of their families, friends and relatives. They should not be ridiculed for their failure. Without that spirit and desire to go ahead, our country would not be what it is today. Unfortunately, in 1982 there were 10,765 business bankruptcies, 410 farm bankruptcies and over 30,000 personal bankruptcies. Losses to business and farm bankruptcies in 1982 amounted to $2.33 billion.
That is very unfortunate. A lot of those people who failed in 1982, given the opportunity and environment, because they are enterprisers and risk-takers, if allowed to have the reward for their endeavours will take the risk again. They will continue to strive for success. If the Government provides the environment and the ability to those people to start again as we, hopefully, come out of this recession, they will survive and contribute to the employment of this country.
Under this Bill, any small farm can have $100,000 outstanding at one time. Let us look at what $100,000 does when used by an enterpriser, a small-businessman. Each $100,000 of equity capital invested in 1979 averaged $310,000 in exports for this country, $100,000 in expenditures for research and $11,000 in corporate, property and personal income taxes to the different levels of Government. That is what $100,000 taken in equity and placed in a small business generated in 1979 in Canada.
By drawing this to the attention of the Government, we are not criticizing this Bill. Indeed, we support it. However, there is one shortfall that could be drawn to the Government's attention. The money available under this Act cannot be used for operating expenses. It cannot be used to carry inventory. For many small businesses, the total cost of their operation is in their inventory. If this Bill could be changed so that small businesses can borrow against their operating cost, it would certainly help.
When I look at this $100,000, I think of all the small businesses in my riding that would be assisted by the injection of that amount of money. Service stations, small grocery stores, welders, farming operations, any number of small businesses, welders, could benefit. If they are going to invest this money and have this assistance from the Government, why in the budget which the Government brought forward did it cut in half the capital cost allowance for the first year for investments? The total cost to small, medium and large businesses is estimated to be in excess of $3 billion. That $3 billion is taken right out of businesses in this country. Where

March 25, 1983
Small Businesses Loans Act
was it put? In the midst of this recession, we pray that businesses will invest, continue to expand, upgrade their production and modernize their plants, but the Government cuts $3 billion out of that operation.
Even worse, every other industrialized country went the other way and allowed a larger capital cost allowance to their businesses. In the United States, for example, the margin will be increased by 34 per cent by 1985 for allowances and equipment and furniture, 42 per cent for automobiles and light trucks and 15 per cent for buildings. That is the difference between the United States and Canada for the operator of a business.
We wonder about capital costs. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) was here a few moments ago. The capital cost allowance for business was cut in half, but an extension of the capital cost allowance, a tax concession, is being proposed for the railroads. The railroads will receive an extended tax credit, a capital cost allowance over the next five years, while farmers and small businesses see their capital cost allowance cut in half. Important as the railroad system in this country may be, it does not compare to the importance of small-businessmen and farmers.
When talking about this Bill, we wonder about the criteria that are established and a lot of the red tape that is involved when making application for these grants. I cast my mind back to last June when a trucking company by the name of Maislin had over $34 million guaranteed by this Government, indeed by the taxpayers of Canada. Maislin was given $34 million in guarantees on unaudited financial statements for the year 1981. That was in July, 1982. On September 14, 1982, over a month later, the Government received the first audited financial statement for that company. That can only happen to friends of the Government. It does not happen to those men and women who operate small businesses and risk their capital.
Over 2,000 employees of Maislin are employed in the United States and 800 are employed in Canada. Therefore, Canadian taxpayers are subsidizing the American teamsters driving Maislin trucks. The operators in the United States are subsidized by taxpayers in this country who are struggling to get ahead and have to use this Small Businesses Loans Act to borrow funds.
When we consider employment and ability to expand, the truckers of Canada are only operating at 60 per cent capacity. Therefore, one has to wonder why it was one company, the only company in the trucking industry, the only service company in Canada, which received a loan guarantee of $34 million from this Government.
I know we will be moving quickly along with this Bill, Mr. Speaker, but I would just like to suggest that in a country as large and expansive as Canada, if you wish to cut the costs- because movement is so important in our country-one place this Government could start which would assist every single business in Canada would be to reduce the take by the federal Government of the tax on fuel.
I would just like to talk briefly about one gallon of fuel. On one gallon of fuel which a farmer now uses in Canada, 69 cents, or 44 per cent, goes in federal tax. Excise tax is seven cents a gallon. Granted, that is refundable. You have to go through a lot of red tape; you have to fill out a lot of forms; you pay it out and you wait for it. Then the people from Revenue Canada come out and do an audit to make sure you are not telling a story. But eventually you get your seven cents. But there is a 9 per cent federal sales tax, which is 15 cents a gallon. There is a petroleum compensation charge which is 18 cents a gallon. That is a familiar figure, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian ownership charge is 4 cents a gallon. Petroleum and gas revenue tax is 7 cents a gallon. And the corporate tax is 18 cents. There are two 18-cent charges in there. That comes to a total of 69 cents a gallon, Mr. Speaker. If you deduct 7 cents a gallon, that is still 62 cents a gallon which is a federal tax. If this tax was removed, in a country the size of Canada, where movement of goods and people are so important to the economy, it would do more good than any other Act that I can think of which we have debated lately in this House.
I would like to move now, Mr. Speaker, that we proceed to the Committee of the Whole and continue the study of this Bill.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, considered in Committee, reported, read the third time and passed.
